title: Chlorophyll and starch: how a leaf catches sunlight and keeps it as food

summary.text: Leaves picked at sunset and at sunrise look the same, but an iodine test shows the sunset leaf holds far more starch. Where does the starch go at night? In this lesson you will test real leaves for starch, check a white patch, and trace your meal back to the Sun.
summary.art: Two leaves that look the same lying on a white plate, one labelled sunset and one labelled sunrise, with a dropper of brown iodine above them.

intro.hook: Think of everything you ate yesterday. Was there one food that did not need sunlight? Say what you think, and why.
intro.text: Most people find this hard to answer. Rice and dal are plants, so they needed sunlight. But what about an egg, a fish or a mushroom? In the first activity, Plate to Sun, you follow each food on a real plate backwards and see where the trail ends. After that you test real leaves. You find out what chlorophyll does, where a leaf keeps the food it makes, and what happens to that food at night. You also meet the few living beings on Earth whose food does not start with sunlight.
intro.art: A steel plate with rice, sambar, a boiled egg, a piece of fish and curd, with a thin dotted line leading from each food towards a small Sun in the corner.

outcomes: By the end I can say what chlorophyll is, where it sits in a leaf, and what it does with light.
By the end I can test a leaf for starch safely, and say why each step of the test is needed.
By the end I can run a fair test on leaves picked at dawn and at dusk, and explain the result.
By the end I can explain why a leaf makes starch only where it has chlorophyll.
By the end I can say what a plant does with sugar and starch, by day and by night.
By the end I can trace almost any food back to sunlight caught by a plant, an alga or a cyanobacterium.
By the end I can name living beings whose food does not start with sunlight, and say how they are fed.
By the end I can say what scientists still do not know about chlorophyll and starch.

terms.meaning: Photosynthesis is the way plants, algae and cyanobacteria make sugar from carbon dioxide and water, using the energy of light. Oxygen is left over.
terms.example: A hibiscus leaf in the morning sun is photosynthesising.
terms.art: A leaf in sunlight with arrows for carbon dioxide and water going in, and sugar and oxygen coming out.

terms.meaning: Chlorophyll is the green pigment in leaves. It catches light, which is the first step of photosynthesis.
terms.example: Palak leaves are dark green because their cells are packed with chlorophyll.
terms.art: A bunch of dark green palak beside a glass of green liquid made from the leaves.

terms.meaning: A pigment is a substance that takes in some colours of light and sends back others. The colours it sends back are the colour we see.
terms.example: Haldi is yellow because of a pigment that sends back yellow light.
terms.art: Small heaps of haldi, kumkum and crushed green leaf side by side.

terms.meaning: A chloroplast is a tiny green body inside a plant cell. All of the cell's chlorophyll is inside its chloroplasts, and photosynthesis happens there.
terms.example: One cell near the top of a leaf can hold dozens of chloroplasts.
terms.art: A box-shaped leaf cell seen close up, with many small green ovals inside it.

terms.meaning: A photon is one tiny packet of light energy. Light always arrives as photons.
terms.example: A photon leaves the Sun and reaches a leaf on Earth about eight minutes later.
terms.art: A row of tiny bright dots travelling from the Sun to a leaf.

terms.meaning: An electron is a very small particle with an electric charge. Every atom has electrons.
terms.example: When chlorophyll catches a photon, one of its electrons gains the photon's energy.
terms.art: A simple atom drawing with one electron jumping to a higher ring.

terms.meaning: Glucose is a simple sugar. It is the sugar most living cells use for energy.
terms.example: The glucose powder sold at a medical shop is the same sugar a leaf makes.
terms.art: A small six-sided ring drawn as one glucose unit, beside a packet of glucose powder.

terms.meaning: Starch is a long chain of thousands of glucose units joined together. Plants make it to store food, because starch does not dissolve in water.
terms.example: Rice, potato, tapioca and ragi are full of starch.
terms.art: A long coiled chain of small six-sided rings, beside a bowl of rice and a potato.

terms.meaning: Sucrose is the sugar that travels inside a plant. It is the same sugar as the white sugar in your kitchen.
terms.example: Sugarcane stems are sweet because the plant stores sucrose in them.
terms.art: A stalk of sugarcane beside a spoon of white sugar.

terms.meaning: Phloem is the set of thin living tubes that carry sucrose from the leaves to every other part of a plant.
terms.example: Sucrose made in a mango leaf travels through the phloem to the growing mango.
terms.art: A plant with thin tubes drawn from a leaf down to the roots and up to a fruit.

terms.meaning: The iodine test is a test for starch. Brown iodine solution turns blue-black where it touches starch.
terms.example: A drop of iodine on a slice of raw potato turns blue-black within seconds.
terms.art: A slice of potato on a white plate with one blue-black spot where a brown drop fell.

terms.meaning: A variegated leaf is a leaf with patches of different colours, often green and white. The white patches have no chlorophyll.
terms.example: Many hibiscus and bougainvillea plants in nurseries have green and white leaves.
terms.art: One leaf with a green middle and a cream-white edge.

terms.meaning: A producer is a living being that makes their own food from things that are not food. Plants, algae and cyanobacteria are producers.
terms.example: A paddy plant is a producer. They make rice grains from air, water and sunlight.
terms.art: A paddy plant in sunlight with a full head of grain.

terms.meaning: A consumer is a living being that gets food by eating other living beings or what they made. All animals, including humans, are consumers.
terms.example: A hen eating grain and a child eating the hen's egg are both consumers.
terms.art: A hen pecking grain beside a child holding a boiled egg.

terms.meaning: Algae are simple living beings that photosynthesise. Most live in water, and seaweeds are large algae. One of them is called an alga.
terms.example: The green film on a wet wall in the monsoon is made of algae.
terms.art: A wet garden wall with a green film, and a close-up circle showing tiny green cells.

terms.meaning: Cyanobacteria are bacteria that photosynthesise. They have chlorophyll but are far smaller than a plant cell.
terms.example: Cyanobacteria floating in the sea do a large share of the photosynthesis on Earth.
terms.art: A drop of sea water with a zoom-in circle showing tiny blue-green dots and short chains.

terms.meaning: Fluorescence is light given out by a substance just after it has caught light of another colour.
terms.example: Chlorophyll dissolved in spirit glows dull red when violet light shines on it.
terms.art: A glass of green liquid in a dark room glowing red along the beam of a small torch.

terms.meaning: Chemical energy is energy held in the way atoms are joined together. Food, wood and petrol all hold chemical energy.
terms.example: The chemical energy in a banana lets you run across the playground.
terms.art: A banana and a running child joined by an arrow.

terms.meaning: Chemosynthesis is a way of making food using energy from chemicals, not from light. Some bacteria do this.
terms.example: Bacteria at hot springs on the deep sea floor make food by chemosynthesis.
terms.art: A dark sea floor with a hot spring, and tall tubeworms growing beside it.

explanations.concept: Chlorophyll: the green pigment that catches light
explanations.definition: Chlorophyll is the green pigment in plants, algae and cyanobacteria. It catches light, and that is the first step of photosynthesis.
explanations.description: A pigment takes in some colours of light and sends back others. Chlorophyll takes in mostly red and blue light. It sends back more of the green light, and that is why leaves look green to us. A leaf still catches a good part of the green light, only less than the red and the blue. Chlorophyll is a molecule, which means a group of atoms joined together. One chlorophyll molecule has about 137 atoms of carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen, arranged around one single atom of magnesium. So a plant needs a little nitrogen and magnesium from the soil to make chlorophyll. A plant that is short of either turns yellow. Chlorophyll is not spread all through a leaf. It sits inside chloroplasts, the tiny green bodies inside leaf cells. Leaves have two main kinds, called chlorophyll a and chlorophyll b. They take in slightly different shades of red and blue, so together they catch more of the light.
examples: In the starch test, the spirit turns green. That green is chlorophyll that has dissolved out of the leaf.
Before an old leaf falls, the plant takes the chlorophyll apart and moves much of the nitrogen to younger leaves. The leaf turns yellow because the yellow pigments are left behind.
A moong sprout grown in a dark cupboard is pale yellow. Most plants make chlorophyll only after they sense light.
explanations.art: A green leaf with a zoom-in circle showing leaf cells, and a second zoom-in showing green chloroplasts inside one cell.

explanations.concept: What happens when chlorophyll catches light
explanations.definition: When a chlorophyll molecule catches a photon, one of its electrons gains the photon's energy. In a living leaf that energy is passed on and used. In a jar it comes straight back out as heat and red light.
explanations.description: Light arrives in tiny packets of energy called photons. When chlorophyll catches a photon, one of its electrons is lifted to a higher energy level. The electron now holds the photon's energy, but only for an instant. What happens next depends on where the chlorophyll is. In a living leaf, chlorophyll molecules sit close together in thin skins inside the chloroplast. A few hundred of them work as one team around a spot called a reaction centre. The energy hops from one chlorophyll to the next in trillionths of a second, until it reaches the reaction centre. There an electron leaves its chlorophyll and is handed along a chain of other molecules. Its energy is used to build sugar. The chlorophyll takes a new electron from water. This splits the water, and oxygen is left over. Now take chlorophyll out of the leaf and dissolve it in spirit. It has no neighbours to hand the energy to. The electron falls back within a few billionths of a second, and the energy comes out as heat and as a dull red light. This red light is called fluorescence.
examples: In the Red Glow activity, green leaf liquid glows red in violet light. The chlorophyll is catching light and has nowhere to send the energy.
A living leaf glows red too, but very faintly. Only about 1 or 2 of every 100 photons a leaf catches come back out as red light.
The oxygen you are breathing now was left over when chlorophyll took electrons from water.
explanations.art: Two drawings side by side: in a leaf, energy hopping along a row of green molecules to a centre, and in a jar, one green molecule giving off a red glow.

explanations.concept: Chlorophyll catches the light, but it does not build the sugar
explanations.definition: Chlorophyll only catches light energy. The sugar is built by other parts of the chloroplast, using that energy and carbon dioxide from the air.
explanations.description: Many books say 'chlorophyll makes food'. That is a shortcut, and it is not quite true. A chloroplast has two parts that work together. In the thin green skins, chlorophyll catches light and water is split. The energy is loaded onto small carrier molecules. These carriers move into the watery part of the chloroplast. There, special proteins called enzymes take carbon dioxide from the air and join it into sugar, using the energy from the carriers. An enzyme is a protein that makes one chemical change happen quickly. So making food needs the whole living chloroplast: chlorophyll, water, enzymes, carbon dioxide and light. Take any one away and no sugar is made.
examples: A rooftop solar panel catches light, but the pump does the lifting of water. In a leaf, chlorophyll is the catcher and the enzymes are the builders.
Chlorophyll in a jar of spirit catches light and makes no sugar at all, because the rest of the chloroplast is missing.
A leaf kept in bright light in a sealed bag with no carbon dioxide makes no starch, even though the chlorophyll is working.
explanations.art: A cut-open chloroplast showing stacks of thin green skins catching light, and the watery space around them where small sugar shapes are being put together.

explanations.definition: Photosynthesis turns light energy into chemical energy. Chemical energy is energy held in the way atoms are joined.
explanations.description: Carbon dioxide and water are low-energy substances. They do not burn, and no living being can get energy from them. Photosynthesis uses the energy of light to pull them apart and join their atoms in a new way, as sugar and oxygen. Sugar and oxygen together hold more energy than the carbon dioxide and water did. When sugar and oxygen meet again and react, they turn back into carbon dioxide and water, and the energy comes out. This happens quickly in a flame. It happens slowly and gently in every living cell, where it is called respiration. People often say 'the energy is in the sugar'. That is nearly right. To be exact, the energy is in sugar and oxygen kept apart from each other. The plant makes both. The sugar stays in the plant, and the oxygen waits in the air.
examples: A dry coconut shell burns with a hot flame. The heat is sunlight energy that the palm's leaves caught years ago.
You feel warm after running. Your cells are joining sugar with oxygen, and part of the energy comes out as heat.
A sealed tin of sugar keeps its energy for years, because the sugar and the oxygen are not reacting.
explanations.art: A simple hill drawing: carbon dioxide and water at the bottom, an arrow of sunlight pushing them up to sugar and oxygen at the top, and a second arrow rolling back down labelled energy out.

explanations.concept: Sugar for now, starch for later, sucrose for travel
explanations.definition: A leaf makes sugar in the light. The plant uses some at once, stores some in the leaf as starch, and sends some to the rest of the plant as sucrose.
explanations.description: On a sunny day a leaf makes sugar faster than the plant can use it. Sugar dissolves in water. A cell full of dissolved sugar would pull in more and more water and swell. So the chloroplast joins thousands of glucose units into long chains of starch. Starch does not dissolve. It sits in the chloroplast as tiny hard grains that take up little room. This leaf starch is what your iodine test finds. For travel, the plant makes a different sugar called sucrose. Sucrose moves through thin living tubes called phloem to every part that makes no food: roots, buds, flowers, fruits and seeds. Those parts use the sucrose to live and grow, or they store it again. Rice grains, potatoes and tapioca roots store it as starch. Sugarcane stems and ripe fruits store it as sugar. Coconuts and groundnuts store it as oil.
examples: A tapioca root grows underground in the dark. Every grain of starch in the root was made as sugar in the leaves above.
In the Banana Clock activity, a raw banana turns blue-black with iodine and a ripe one hardly changes. The fruit turns stored starch back into sugar as it ripens.
White sugar is sucrose taken from sugarcane. It is the same travelling sugar that flows in the phloem of every tree.
explanations.art: A plant drawn with a leaf making sugar, starch grains shown inside the leaf, and arrows of sucrose flowing down to a fat root and up to a fruit.

explanations.concept: How a leaf makes the day's starch last all night
explanations.definition: A plant makes food only in the light, but their cells need energy all night too. So the leaf breaks down its starch slowly through the night and sends the sugar to the rest of the plant.
explanations.description: At dusk a leaf is full of starch. At dawn most of it is gone. This is what the Dawn Leaf, Dusk Leaf experiment tests. Scientists have measured it hour by hour in a small plant called thale cress, a relative of mustard. The leaf uses up starch at a steady rate all night. By dawn about 95 parts of every 100 are gone, and the plant has not run short. Then the scientists switched off the lights four hours early. The plants used their starch more slowly that night, and it still lasted until dawn. Plants whose inner daily clock is damaged get this wrong. They run out of starch before dawn and grow less. So a plant measures how much starch they have and how long the night will be, and sets the speed to match. Everyone agrees that this happens. How the plant does it is still argued over. Other plants may do it differently, and some store sugar instead of starch.
examples: If a leaf has 60 units of starch and 12 hours of night, a steady rate of 5 units an hour uses all 60 by dawn.
A potted tulsi plant kept in a dark cupboard for two days uses up nearly all the starch in their leaves. That is why school books say to 'destarch' a plant in the dark before a test.
You do something like this too. Your liver stores sugar after dinner and lets it out slowly while you sleep.

perspectives.who: Alison Smith, Martin Howard and their team at the John Innes Centre in England (2013)
perspectives.explanation: The plant does a kind of division. Two chemicals in the leaf keep track of the amount of starch and the time left until dawn. The rate of use is the first divided by the second.

perspectives.who: Other plant scientists, including Akiko Satake's group in Japan
perspectives.explanation: The plant needs no division. The amount of sugar in the leaf nudges the plant's daily clock forward or back, and the clock controls how fast starch is used. That simple loop gives nearly the same result.

explanations.art: A leaf at dusk full of dark starch grains, the same leaf at midnight half full, and the same leaf at dawn nearly empty, with a moon moving across the three pictures.

explanations.concept: Why the starch test has four steps
explanations.definition: The starch test on a leaf uses hot water, then spirit, then a rinse, then iodine. Each step does one job.
explanations.description: First the leaf goes into very hot water for a minute. This kills the leaf cells, so they stop using up starch. It also breaks the thin skin around each cell, so that liquids can get in and out. Second, the leaf sits in warm spirit. Chlorophyll does not dissolve in water, but it does dissolve in spirit. The spirit turns green and the leaf turns pale. Now a colour change will be easy to see. Third, the leaf is rinsed in warm water, because spirit leaves it stiff and brittle. Fourth, brown iodine solution is poured on. Starch is a long chain that coils like a spring. Iodine particles slip inside the coil and line up in a row. A row of iodine inside a starch coil takes in light differently from loose iodine, and looks blue-black. Where there is no starch, the iodine stays yellow-brown. The test shows starch, not sugar. Sugar gives no colour with iodine.
examples: A drop of iodine on cooked rice goes blue-black at once. A drop on a pinch of sugar stays brown.
If you skip the spirit, a dark green leaf looks almost the same before and after iodine.
Onion leaves stay brown in the test. Onion plants store sugar in their leaves, not starch.
explanations.art: Four small pictures in a row: a leaf in hot water, a leaf in a tumbler of green spirit, a pale leaf being rinsed, and the pale leaf turning blue-black under a dropper.

explanations.definition: A part of a plant that has no chlorophyll cannot catch light, so no sugar or starch is made there. It lives on sugar sent from the green parts.
explanations.description: Some leaves have white or cream patches. These are called variegated leaves. The cells in the white patches are alive, but their chloroplasts have no chlorophyll. In the White Patch experiment, iodine turns the green parts blue-black and leaves the white parts brown. The white cells are kept alive by sucrose that flows in from the green cells beside them. Roots, flower petals and the inside of a tree trunk live the same way. Now and then a seed sprouts into a seedling that is white all over. This is called an albino seedling. They grow well for a few weeks on the food stored in the seed. When the seed is empty they die, however much light, water and manure they are given. A few plants have given up chlorophyll and live by taking food from others. Dodder, called amarbel in Hindi, is a tangle of yellow threads on roadside hedges. Dodder pushes tiny suckers into a green plant and drinks their sucrose.
examples: A variegated hibiscus grows more slowly than an all-green one. They have less green to feed the same size of plant.
The bright yellow or red ball of a moon cactus has no chlorophyll. Nurseries join it onto a green cactus stem, and the green stem feeds both.
You have no chlorophyll either. Like the white patch, every animal is fed by green cells somewhere else.
explanations.art: A green and white leaf before the test, and the same leaf after the test with the green parts now blue-black and the white parts pale brown.

explanations.concept: Hidden green: red, purple and yellow leaves
explanations.definition: A leaf that looks red or purple still has chlorophyll. A second pigment covers the green.
explanations.description: Leaves hold other pigments besides chlorophyll. Red and purple pigments sit dissolved in the watery sap of the cells. Yellow and orange pigments, called carotenoids, sit in the chloroplasts next to the chlorophyll. Carotenoids catch some blue and green light and pass the energy on to chlorophyll. They also take up extra energy in very bright light, so the chlorophyll is not harmed. In a red amaranth leaf there is so much red pigment that we cannot see the green under it. The Green Under Red activity shows this. Hot water takes out the red pigment, because the red pigment dissolves in water. The chlorophyll stays behind, because it does not, and the leaf turns green. Red leaves photosynthesise and give a blue-black starch test. Only the truly white parts of a leaf do not.
examples: Red cheera in Kerala and lal saag in Bengal are red amaranth leaves. The cooking water turns pink and the cooked leaves look green.
Young mango and peepal leaves are coppery red. Scientists think the red pigment shades the new chlorophyll while the leaf is still soft.
A coleus leaf can be purple, red and green at once. All three parts usually pass the starch test.
explanations.art: A red amaranth leaf beside a tumbler of pink water with a dull green leaf lying in it.

explanations.concept: Almost all food starts with caught sunlight
explanations.definition: Producers make food from things that are not food. Almost all producers on Earth use sunlight to do it. Every consumer lives on what producers made.
explanations.description: Follow any food backwards and ask each time, 'and what did they eat?' The trail nearly always ends at a producer. On land the producers are mostly plants. In the sea they are mostly algae and cyanobacteria, which are tiny living beings that float near the surface. Cyanobacteria are bacteria that photosynthesise. The sea's producers do about half of all the photosynthesis on Earth. So 'food comes from plants' is a simplification. The fuller picture is that food comes from every living being that has chlorophyll. A sardine ate tiny animals that ate algae. A hen ate grain. A mushroom fed on dead straw. Each step passes on only a part of the energy, because every eater uses most of their food to stay alive. Producers catch only a small share of the sunlight that reaches the Earth, roughly one part in a thousand. All animals, fungi and most bacteria live on that share.
examples: Curd: sunlight was caught by grass, the cow ate the grass and made milk, and bacteria turned the milk into curd.
Fish curry in Kochi: sunlight was caught by algae in the Arabian Sea, small animals ate the algae, and the fish ate them.
Salt and water are on your plate too, but they give no energy. They are not food in this sense, and they do not come from sunlight.
explanations.art: A Sun at the top with lines running down to a paddy plant, a patch of grass and tiny sea algae, and from those to a plate of rice, a cow, a fish and finally a child.

explanations.concept: The 'almost': living beings fed by chemicals
explanations.definition: A few living beings get their energy from chemicals that come out of rock, not from light. This is called chemosynthesis.
explanations.description: Deep in the sea, far below where any sunlight reaches, hot water full of dissolved chemicals pours out of cracks in the sea floor. Bacteria there make sugar from carbon dioxide, as plants do. But their energy comes from a chemical in the hot water called hydrogen sulphide, the gas that smells of rotten eggs. Giant tubeworms, clams and crabs live around these hot springs. The tubeworms have no mouth. Bacteria live inside their bodies and feed them. Even here the Sun plays a part. Most of these bacteria need oxygen to use the hydrogen sulphide, and that oxygen was made by photosynthesis far above. A few microbes do without the Sun completely. In 2008 scientists described bacteria living in water inside rock 2.8 kilometres down a South African gold mine. They live on hydrogen that forms when natural radioactivity in the rock splits water. This is why we say 'almost all' food starts with sunlight, and not 'all'.
examples: Giant tubeworms at deep-sea hot springs grow up to about 2 metres long, fed only by the bacteria inside them.
In the gold mine, the bacteria have been cut off from sunlight for millions of years.
Some scientists think life on Earth may have started at such hot springs, before any living being could use light. Nobody knows yet.
explanations.art: A dark sea floor with a chimney of rock pouring out cloudy hot water, surrounded by tall white tubes with red tips, and no light from above.

explanations.definition: Living leaves give off a very faint red glow while they photosynthesise. Satellites can measure this glow from space.
explanations.description: You read that chlorophyll in a jar glows red, and that a living leaf glows red very faintly. The glow from one leaf is far too dim for your eyes in daylight. But a whole forest or a field of paddy has billions of leaves. Since 2011, scientists have used satellites to measure this faint red glow over the whole Earth. Where the glow is strong, leaves are catching a lot of light and making a lot of sugar. Where it fades, the plants are short of water, too cold or too hot. So the glow works as a health report for the green cover of the Earth. Scientists use it to watch crops, forests and droughts. In India the glow rises across the country after the monsoon arrives and the fields turn green.
examples: The same red glow that you see in a glass in the Red Glow activity is what the satellites measure.
The glow over the paddy fields of the Kaveri delta rises as the crop grows and falls after harvest.
The sea's algae glow as well, and satellites map them too.
explanations.art: A satellite above the Earth looking down at India, with green land giving off a soft red haze.

explanations.definition: Our picture of chlorophyll and starch was built by many people over about 200 years.
explanations.description: In 1817 two French chemists, Pierre-Joseph Pelletier and Joseph Bienaimé Caventou, took the green substance out of leaves and named it chlorophyll, from Greek words for 'green' and 'leaf'. In 1845 the German doctor Julius Robert Mayer wrote that plants take in the energy of light and store it as chemical energy. In the 1860s Julius von Sachs, also in Germany, used the iodine test on leaves. He showed that starch grains appear inside chloroplasts, and only when the leaf is in light. Richard Willstätter showed that every chlorophyll molecule holds one atom of magnesium, and won a Nobel Prize in 1915. Jagadish Chandra Bose in Kolkata built instruments to record photosynthesis in water plants, and wrote a book on it in 1924. Govindjee, born in Allahabad in 1932, spent his working life at the University of Illinois studying how chlorophyll handles light and why it glows. Rajni Govindjee worked on photosynthesis in the same laboratory. In 2013 Alison Smith and her team in England showed how carefully a leaf shares out its starch through the night.
examples: The word chlorophyll is just over 200 years old. The pigment itself is more than two billion years old.
The iodine test you do at home is the test Sachs used on leaves in the 1860s.
Colleen Cavanaugh was a student in 1981 when she worked out how tubeworms at deep-sea hot springs are fed.
explanations.art: A timeline with small portraits and dates from 1817 to 2013, ending with a leaf under a dropper of iodine.

agreed.text: Chlorophyll catches mostly red and blue light, and this is the first step of photosynthesis.
agreed.evidence: When light is split into colours and shone on algae, the most oxygen is made in the red and the blue. Theodor Engelmann showed this in 1882, and it has been measured many times since.

agreed.text: Every chlorophyll molecule has one atom of magnesium at its centre.
agreed.evidence: Richard Willstätter found magnesium in the chlorophyll of every plant he tested, before 1915. The full shape of the molecule was worked out by 1940, and chemists built it in a laboratory in 1960.

agreed.text: Starch forms in a leaf only where there is chlorophyll and only when there is light.
agreed.evidence: Iodine tests on covered leaves and on variegated leaves show this. Julius von Sachs did the first such tests in the 1860s, and you can repeat them at home.

agreed.text: A leaf builds up starch by day and uses most of it up by the next dawn.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have measured the starch in leaves hour by hour in many plants. In thale cress about 95 parts in 100 are used by dawn.

agreed.text: The sea's algae and cyanobacteria do about half of the photosynthesis on Earth.
agreed.evidence: Satellites measure the chlorophyll in sea water by its colour. From this, Christopher Field and others worked out in 1998 that the sea and the land each do about half.

agreed.text: A few living beings are fed by chemosynthesis, with energy from chemicals and not from light.
agreed.evidence: Animals crowded around deep-sea hot springs were first seen in 1977. Bacteria that feed them were found inside tubeworms in 1981.

challenging.for: Without chlorophyll no food is made. White patches on a leaf make no starch.
challenging.against: Chlorophyll only catches the light. Enzymes in another part of the chloroplast build the sugar. Chlorophyll in a jar catches light and makes no food at all.
challenging.context: This card is about a line in many books: that chlorophyll is the thing that makes a plant's food.

challenging.claim: All life on Earth depends on the Sun.
challenging.for: Nearly every food chain starts with sunlight caught by a plant, an alga or a cyanobacterium. Even most deep-sea bacteria use oxygen that photosynthesis made.
challenging.against: Some microbes deep inside rock live on hydrogen made by natural radioactivity. They need nothing from the Sun. So the true word is 'almost all'.
challenging.context: This card is about the saying that every living being depends on the Sun.

challenging.claim: A red or purple leaf has no chlorophyll.
challenging.who: What many people think when they see a red plant
challenging.for: The leaf does not look green at all.
challenging.against: Hot water takes the red pigment out of a red amaranth leaf, and the leaf turns green. Red leaves also give a blue-black starch test. The chlorophyll was there, under the red.
challenging.context: This card is about red and purple leaves, such as red amaranth and coleus, and whether they have chlorophyll.

challenging.claim: A plant does arithmetic at night to share out their starch.
challenging.who: Alison Smith, Martin Howard and their team, 2013
challenging.for: Thale cress plants use starch at a steady rate that lasts almost exactly until dawn. When night comes four hours early, they slow down at once and still last until dawn.
challenging.against: Other scientists agree with the measurements, but say a simpler loop between sugar and the plant's daily clock explains them. They say no division is needed.
challenging.context: This card is about how a leaf makes the day's starch last through the night. One team says the plant does a kind of division.

challenging.claim: A green sea slug can live on sunlight like a plant.
challenging.who: Reports about the sea slug Elysia chlorotica
challenging.for: This slug eats algae and keeps the algae's chloroplasts alive in their own body for months. The slug turns green, and the chloroplasts go on photosynthesising.
challenging.against: In 2014, scientists kept related green slugs in the dark, and they lived as long as slugs kept in the light. So the slugs may use the chloroplasts mainly as a food store.
challenging.context: This card is about a green sea slug who takes chloroplasts from the algae they eat.

challenging.claim: Plants are the only living beings that make food from light.
challenging.for: On land, nearly all the photosynthesis we can see is done by plants.
challenging.against: Algae and cyanobacteria do about half of all photosynthesis, and they are not plants. Reef corals are animals, but algae live inside their bodies and make most of their food.
challenging.context: This card is about who makes food from light. Many people say only plants do.

big_questions.q: Chlorophyll in a jar catches light and makes no food. So what really makes the food: the chlorophyll, or the whole living leaf?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the leaf has that the jar does not.

big_questions.q: A leaf uses up its starch at a speed that just lasts until dawn. Is that planning? How would you decide?
big_questions.hint: What would a plant with no way of measuring do on a night that came early?

big_questions.q: You have no chlorophyll. Are you more like the green part of a variegated leaf or the white part?
big_questions.hint: Think about where the white patch gets sugar from, and where you get yours.

big_questions.q: Producers catch about one part in a thousand of the sunlight that reaches the Earth. Humans take about a quarter of what land plants grow each year. Is that a fair share for one kind of animal?
big_questions.hint: Think about who else has to live on the rest.

big_questions.q: A few microbes deep in rock have never used sunlight. If we find life on another world, should we look for green leaves, or for something else?
big_questions.hint: Think about places with no sunlight, such as the sea under the ice of Jupiter's moon Europa.

big_questions.q: People named chlorophyll only about 200 years ago. Leaves had been green for hundreds of millions of years before that. What else might be in plain sight that nobody has named yet?
big_questions.hint: Think about things you see every day and have never asked about.

story.title: The White Seedling
story.note: A made-up story. Devika, Shobha Ammayi and their nursery are imagined. Mannuthy, near Thrissur in Kerala, is a real place with many plant nurseries. The science is real. Seedlings with no chlorophyll, called albino seedlings, turn up now and then in many kinds of plants. They live only as long as the food in the seed lasts. The moon cactus is a real plant sold in nurseries. Its coloured top has no chlorophyll and is joined onto a green cactus stem.
text: The jackfruit seeds came up in the third week of June, when the rain had settled over Mannuthy. Devika counted them every morning before school. She had pushed forty seeds into forty black bags with her own thumb. Thirty-six had come up.
Thirty-five were green. One was white.

Not pale green. White, like the inside of a tender coconut. The stem was white. The two small leaves were white, with a little pink where the veins ran. Among the rows of ordinary seedlings they stood out like a candle in a dark room.
'Ammayi! Come and see!'
Her aunt Shobha came down the path between the benches, wiping her hands on her sari. She had run this nursery for twenty years. She bent over the bag and looked for a long time.
'I have seen four of these,' she said. 'In twenty years.'
'Are they sick?'
'No. They were born this way.'
'Can I keep them?'
'You planted them. They are yours.' Ammayi straightened up. 'Look after them well. And watch closely.'

Devika named the seedling Nilavu, which means moonlight. She moved the bag to the best place in the nursery, the bench by the gate, where the morning sun came first. She gave Nilavu rainwater from the brass uruli and a pinch of old cow dung manure. She turned the bag a little each day, so that both leaves had their share of the light.

For two weeks Nilavu grew as fast as any of the green ones. A third leaf opened, as white as the first two. Customers stopped at the gate to look. A woman from Thrissur offered five hundred rupees. Devika said no before Ammayi could answer.
In the fourth week, Nilavu stopped.

The green seedlings opened a fourth leaf and then a fifth, dark and shining. Nilavu's third leaf began to hang down. Devika gave more water. The leaf hung lower. She carried the bag into the open yard for more sun, and by evening the edges of the leaves had gone brown. She carried the bag back into the shade. She soaked manure in a bucket and poured the brown water round the stem. Nothing helped.
On Saturday she stood in front of her aunt with the bag in both hands.
'I did everything. The same soil as the others. The same water. More sun than anyone.'
'You did,' said Ammayi. 'Everything you could give, you gave.'
'Then what is missing?'
Ammayi did not answer. She spread a newspaper on the bench. She took Nilavu's bag and the bag of a green seedling, and tipped each one out gently, soil and all.
'Look at the seeds.'

Under each seedling the jackfruit seed was still there, joined to the bottom of the stem. Devika had last seen those seeds fat and smooth and heavy. Now both were brown and wrinkled. She pressed one with her finger. It was hollow, like a pod with nothing in it.
'Both of them have been eating from the seed,' said Ammayi. 'The mother tree packs every seed full, like a tiffin box. Now both boxes are empty.'
'But the green one is still growing.'
'So where is their food coming from now?'
Devika looked at the green seedling lying on the newspaper. Five leaves, held out flat. She knew this from school. She had only never needed it before.
'From the leaves. The leaves make it, from the light.'
'And Nilavu's leaves?'
Devika looked. The sun was on the white leaves at that moment. It lit them right through, like paper held up to a window. There was nothing in them to stop the light and hold it.
'I gave them more sun than anyone,' she said slowly. 'And they could not catch any of it.'
'Whose sunlight was in the seed?'

'The mother tree's. From last summer.' So Nilavu had lived four weeks on last year's light. All the water and all the manure had been beside the point. It was a hard thing to know. Devika sat down on the upturned bucket and stayed there for a while.

When she looked up, Ammayi was holding a small clay pot from the cactus shelf. In it stood a green stem with three sides, as long as a finger. On top of the stem sat a round ball, bright yellow, with not one speck of green.
'Moon cactus,' said Ammayi. 'How old, do you think?'
Devika shook her head.
'Six years. And in six years the yellow one has not made a single grain of food.'
Devika took the pot and turned it. Where the yellow met the green there was a thin line, like an old scar.
'Somebody joined them,' she said.
'When the yellow one was smaller than your thumbnail. Everything they have grown since then, the green stem caught for them.'
Devika put the pot down very carefully. 'Can we join Nilavu to a green one?'

'A jackfruit this young and this soft? I have never managed it.' Ammayi looked at the white seedling on the newspaper. 'I think it will fail. But we can try tomorrow, with the sharpest blade, if you hold the lamp.'

At one o'clock they ate on the back step, out of the rain. Rice, moru curry, and red cheera from the bed behind the well. Devika took a handful of rice and then stopped with it halfway to her mouth. She was looking at her own hand. Brown skin, pink nails. No green anywhere.
'Ammayi. I am like Nilavu.'
'Hm?'
'No green. I cannot catch any light either. Somebody has to catch it for me.'
Ammayi went on eating. 'And who is your green stem?'

Devika looked at the rice in her hand and the cheera on her plate. She looked at the thirty-five seedlings on the bench, and the old jackfruit tree by the gate, and the wet hills beyond the road, every one of them holding leaves up to the grey sky.
'All of that,' she said.
She ate the rice slowly. Then she went to find the blade.
story.epiphany: For the parent: a plant with no chlorophyll cannot catch light, so no amount of sun, water or manure can feed them. The white seedling lived for four weeks on food that the mother tree had packed into the seed, which was the mother tree's caught sunlight. When that ran out, the seedling had nothing. The green seedlings had begun to make their own food by then. The moon cactus lives for years with no chlorophyll, because a green stem joined to them catches light for both. Every animal, including a child eating rice, is in the same position as the white seedling. We live on light that green cells caught.
ask: Devika gave the white seedling more sun than any other. Why did the extra sun not help?
Both seeds were empty after four weeks. Why was the green seedling still growing?
How does the yellow moon cactus stay alive with no chlorophyll?
Devika said, 'I am like Nilavu.' In what way is that true? In what way is it not?
Whose sunlight was in your breakfast this morning?

games.title: Back to the Sun
games.context: This is a card game about where food comes from. Each card names one food. You say the chain of living beings that leads from the Sun to you, then turn the card to check.

printables.title: 20 food cards to cut out (the chain is on the back)

items.f: Idli. Say the chain from the Sun to you.
items.b: Sun → paddy plant and urad plant → you. Tiny microbes in the batter also fed on the starch. Eaters before you: 0.

items.f: Curd. Say the chain from the Sun to you.
items.b: Sun → grass → cow, who made milk → curd bacteria → you. Eaters before you: 2.

items.f: A boiled egg. Say the chain from the Sun to you.
items.b: Sun → maize and other grain plants → hen → you. Eaters before you: 1.

items.f: Honey. Say the chain from the Sun to you.
items.b: Sun → flowering plants, who made nectar → honeybees → you. Eaters before you: 1.

items.f: Fried sardine (mathi). Say the chain from the Sun to you.
items.b: Sun → tiny sea algae → tiny sea animals → sardine → you. Eaters before you: 2.

items.f: Coconut chutney. Say the chain from the Sun to you.
items.b: Sun → coconut palm → you. The palm stored the sunlight's energy as oil in the coconut. Eaters before you: 0.

items.f: Jaggery. Say the chain from the Sun to you.
items.b: Sun → sugarcane → you. Sugarcane stores sucrose in the stem. Eaters before you: 0.

items.f: Ghee. Say the chain from the Sun to you.
items.b: Sun → grass → cow or buffalo, who made milk → you. Eaters before you: 1.

items.f: Mushroom curry. Say the chain from the Sun to you.
items.b: Sun → paddy plant → dead straw → mushroom, a fungus who feeds on the straw → you. Eaters before you: 1.

items.f: Salt. Say the chain from the Sun to you.
items.b: No chain. Salt is a mineral from sea water or rock. It gives you no energy, and it does not come from sunlight.

items.f: A glass of water. Say the chain from the Sun to you.
items.b: No chain. Water gives you no energy. A plant uses water to make food, but water itself is not made from sunlight.

items.f: Seer fish (vanjaram) curry. Say the chain from the Sun to you.
items.b: Sun → tiny sea algae → tiny sea animals → small fish → seer fish → you. Eaters before you: 3.

items.f: Groundnut chikki. Say the chain from the Sun to you.
items.b: Sun → groundnut plant → you, and Sun → sugarcane → you. Two short chains meet in one sweet. Eaters before you: 0.

items.f: Prawn curry. Say the chain from the Sun to you.
items.b: Sun → algae and bits of dead plants → prawn → you. Eaters before you: 1.

items.f: Chicken biryani. Say the chain from the Sun to you.
items.b: Sun → paddy plant → you, and Sun → grain plants → chicken → you. Eaters before you: 0 for the rice, 1 for the chicken.

items.f: A ripe mango. Say the chain from the Sun to you.
items.b: Sun → mango tree → you. The leaves made sugar and sent it to the fruit as sucrose. Eaters before you: 0.

items.f: Boiled tapioca (kappa). Say the chain from the Sun to you.
items.b: Sun → tapioca plant → you. The leaves made sugar, and the root stored it as starch. Eaters before you: 0.

items.f: Paneer. Say the chain from the Sun to you.
items.b: Sun → grass → cow or buffalo, who made milk → you. Eaters before you: 1.

items.f: A tubeworm's meal at a hot spring on the deep sea floor. Say the chain from the Sun to you.
items.b: No sunlight in this chain. Chemicals from hot rock → bacteria inside the tubeworm → tubeworm. The bacteria do use oxygen that photosynthesis made far above.

items.f: Tea with milk and sugar. Say the chain from the Sun to you.
items.b: Three chains. Sun → tea bush → you. Sun → grass → cow → you. Sun → sugarcane → you. Eaters before you: 0, 1 and 0.

rules: Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile, food side up.
The first player reads the top card aloud. Then they say the chain from the Sun to themselves, one living being at a time.
They also say how many eaters come before them in the chain. A plant or an alga is not an eater.
Turn the card over. A right chain scores 1 point. The right number of eaters scores 1 more point.
Three cards have no chain from the Sun. Saying 'no chain' and giving the reason scores 2 points.
Take turns until all 20 cards are used. The player with the most points wins.
Playing alone: say each chain aloud before you turn the card. Try to reach 30 points out of 40, then play again.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 20 cards. 2. Shuffle them. 3. Put them in a pile, food side up. 4. Keep a paper and pencil for the points.
flow.say: Each card names a food. We will find out what every food starts with. We follow the food backwards, one living being at a time, until we reach the Sun.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Shuffle them. Put them in a pile. Get a pencil for the points.
flow.context: This is the first step of Back to the Sun. Here you set up the cards.

flow.do: 1. Read the top card aloud. 2. Say the chain from the Sun to you. 3. Say how many living beings ate something along the way. 4. Turn the card over and check. 5. Write down the points.
flow.say: Who made this food, and what did they eat? Ask it again for each living being. Stop when you reach one who makes food from light.
flow.kid: Read the card. Say the chain from the Sun to you. Then turn the card and check.

ask.q: Curd has two eaters before you. Who are they?
good: The cow, who ate grass.
The curd bacteria, who fed on the milk.

flow.parent: The chains on the cards are simplified. A real sardine eats algae as well as tiny animals. If your child gives a true chain that differs from the card, give the point.
flow.context: This is the main part of Back to the Sun. Here you say each food's chain and check it.

flow.do: 1. Count the points. 2. Lay all 20 cards out with the chain side up. 3. Sort them into three heaps: a plant or alga first, no chain from the Sun, and no sunlight at all.
flow.say: Look at the heaps. What comes first in nearly every chain? Which cards were different, and why?
flow.kid: Count your points. Sort the cards into three heaps. What starts nearly every chain?

check.q: A mushroom grows in the dark on dead straw. Does the mushroom's food start with sunlight?
options: Yes, because the straw was once a paddy plant
Yes, because mushrooms have chlorophyll
No, because mushrooms grow in the dark
check.why: The mushroom feeds on dead straw, and the paddy plant built that straw with sunlight. Choosing 'no' usually means looking only at where the mushroom lives. The question is where the food came from. Mushrooms have no chlorophyll.

flow.context: This is the last step of Back to the Sun. Here you count points and sort the cards.

games.title: Starch Bank: make the day's food last until dawn
games.context: This is a dice game about a leaf's day and night. You are a plant. By day you collect beans, which stand for starch. At night you must share them out so that they last until dawn.

printables.title: Score sheet for each player (copy it for 6 nights)
items: Did the beans last until dawn?

rules: You need one die and about 40 dry beans or tamarind seeds. Each player is a plant. Each bean is some starch.
A day has three parts: morning, noon and afternoon. Roll the die once for each part and take that many beans.
At dusk you choose how many beans to spend in each part of the night. You must spend the same number in every part.
Each bean you spend at night scores 1 growth point, because the plant grows on it.
If you choose too many and the beans run out before the last part, your plant goes hungry. You score nothing for that night.
Beans left over at dawn stay in your leaf for the next day. They score nothing until you spend them.
Nights 1 to 3 are played with a broken clock. Choose your number first, and only then turn over a night card to see how long the night is.
Nights 4 to 6 are played with a working clock. Turn over the night card first, and then choose your number.
After 6 nights, the plant with the most growth points wins. Playing alone: compare your points for nights 1 to 3 with your points for nights 4 to 6.

setup.art: A child rolling a die on a floor mat beside a bowl of dry beans and a pile of small face-down cards.
setup.caption: 1. Roll the die three times for the day and take that many beans.

setup.art: A turned-over card that says Long night: 5 parts, with 14 beans being shared into five small groups on the mat.
setup.caption: 2. Share your beans equally over the parts of the night.

setup.art: A score sheet with six rows, and a child writing growth points in the last column.
setup.caption: 3. Write your growth points. Play six nights.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 12 night cards, shuffle them and lay them face down. 2. Copy the score sheet for each player. 3. Put the beans in a bowl.
flow.say: You are a plant. By day you make starch. At night you live on it. Each night card shows how many parts the night has. Your job is to make your beans last until dawn.
flow.kid: Cut out the night cards. Shuffle them. Copy the score sheet. Put the beans in a bowl.
flow.context: This is the first step of Starch Bank. Here you set up the cards, the beans and the score sheet.

flow.do: 1. Roll the die three times and take the beans. 2. Each player says how many beans they will spend in each part of the night. 3. Now turn over a night card. 4. Spend the beans, part by part. 5. Write the points. 6. Play three nights like this.
flow.say: Your clock is broken. You do not know how long tonight will be. How many beans will you spend in each part? Why that number?
flow.kid: Roll three times. Take your beans. Choose a number for each part. Then turn the night card.
flow.parent: Nights have 3, 4, 5 or 6 parts. Many children choose a big number and run out on a long night. Let that happen. Put used night cards back and reshuffle if the pile runs out.
flow.context: These are nights 1 to 3 of Starch Bank. Here you choose before you know how long the night is.

flow.do: 1. Roll the die three times and take the beans. 2. Turn over a night card first. 3. Each player divides their beans by the number of parts and says the sum aloud. 4. Spend the beans and write the points. 5. Play three nights like this.
flow.say: Now your clock works, so you know how long the night is. Divide your beans by the parts of the night. What is left over?
flow.kid: Roll three times. Turn the night card first. Divide your beans by the parts. Spend them.

ask.q: You have 14 beans and a night of 4 parts. How many do you spend in each part?
good: 3 in each part, because 4 times 3 is 12.
2 beans are left over for tomorrow.

flow.context: These are nights 4 to 6 of Starch Bank. Here you know how long the night is before you choose.

flow.do: 1. Add the points for nights 1 to 3. 2. Add the points for nights 4 to 6. 3. Compare the two totals.
flow.say: When did your plant grow more: with the broken clock, or with the working clock? What did the clock let you do?
flow.kid: Add your points for nights 1 to 3. Add your points for nights 4 to 6. Which is more?
flow.parent: Real thale cress plants with a damaged daily clock do run out of starch before dawn, and they grow less. With only three nights each way, luck with the die can hide the difference. Play again if it does.

check.q: A leaf has 48 units of starch at dusk, and the night is 12 hours long. Which steady rate uses it all exactly by dawn?
options: 4 units an hour
6 units an hour
12 units an hour
check.why: 48 ÷ 12 = 4. At 4 units an hour the starch lasts exactly 12 hours. At 6 units an hour it would run out after 8 hours, and the plant would go hungry for the last 4.

flow.context: This is the last step of Starch Bank. Here you compare the broken clock with the working clock.

experiments.title: Dawn Leaf, Dusk Leaf: does a leaf hold the same starch at sunrise and at sunset?
experiments.context: In this experiment you pick two leaves from one plant early in the morning, and two more late in the afternoon. You test all four for starch with iodine, to see whether the time of day changes how much starch a leaf holds. You will find out whether a leaf stores food in the day and uses it up at night.
experiments.question: Does a leaf hold more starch at the end of the day, at the end of the night, or the same at both times?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Two leaves are picked at sunrise and two at sunset, from the same plant. Which pair will go darker with iodine: the sunrise pair, the sunset pair, or both the same? Write your guess and your reason for it.
experiments.fair_test: Change only the time of picking. Use one plant. Pick leaves of the same size from the same sunny side. Treat all four leaves in the same tumbler of spirit for the same time, and use the same iodine. Test two leaves from each time, because one leaf alone can be odd.

materials.item: a potted plant with thin, soft leaves that gets direct sun for at least 3 hours a day, such as hibiscus, tulsi, balsam, coleus, mint, or a tomato or chilli plant. Thick, shiny leaves like money plant work badly.
surgical spirit or rubbing alcohol, enough to fill a small steel tumbler one third full. It catches fire easily.
povidone-iodine solution, the brown antiseptic sold at medical shops
a small steel tumbler, a big bowl, tongs or a spoon, and very hot water from a kettle or a pan
a white plate, a small cup, scissors, a small box with a lid, a spoon of cooked rice, a notebook and a pencil

experiments.safety: Surgical spirit catches fire very easily. Never heat it on a stove or near a flame. Warm it only by standing its tumbler in hot water, with the stove switched off. Only a grown-up handles the hot water and the spirit. Iodine stains cloth and must not be swallowed.

schedule.what: Early morning, before the sun reaches the plant: guess, pick two dawn leaves, dip them in hot water and put them in the fridge.
Late afternoon of the same sunny day: pick two dusk leaves, test all four leaves and score them.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for all four leaves. Take a photo of each leaf after the iodine, or draw and colour it. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
