flow.do: 1. Do this early, before sunlight falls on the plant. 2. Look at the plant together. 3. Ask for the guess and the reason. 4. Your child writes both down.
flow.say: We will pick leaves now and again at sunset. Which leaves will hold more starch, or will they be the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the plant. Guess which leaves hold more starch: morning or evening. Say why. Write it down.

good: The leaf makes food all day, so it has more in the evening.
They look the same, so they hold the same.
Any guess with a reason is good.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Choose a day that is forecast to be sunny. The plant should also have had sun the day before.
flow.context: This is the first step of Dawn Leaf, Dusk Leaf. Here you guess before you pick any leaf.

flow.do: 1. Pick two healthy leaves of the same size from the sunny side. 2. Snip a small piece off the tip of each, so you know them later. 3. A grown-up holds them in just-boiled water for 1 minute. 4. Put them in a small closed box in the fridge.
flow.say: These are our dawn leaves. The hot water stops the leaf cells working, so the starch stays as it is now.
flow.kid: Pick two leaves. Snip the tips. A grown-up dips them in hot water. Put them in the fridge.
flow.wait: Wait until late afternoon of the same day
flow.parent: Leaves picked up to an hour after sunrise still work, as long as no direct sun has reached the plant. The snipped tip is the label, because all four leaves look alike once they are pale.
flow.context: This step of Dawn Leaf, Dusk Leaf is done in the early morning. Here you pick and keep the dawn leaves.

flow.do: 1. Between 4 and 5 in the afternoon, pick two more leaves from the same side. Leave their tips whole. 2. A grown-up holds them in just-boiled water for 1 minute. 3. Take the dawn leaves out of the fridge.
flow.say: These are our dusk leaves. They have had a whole day of light. Do they look any different from the dawn leaves?
flow.kid: Pick two more leaves. Do not snip them. A grown-up dips them in hot water. Compare all four.
flow.parent: All four leaves look the same shade of dull green at this point. That is the puzzle: you cannot see starch.
flow.context: This step of Dawn Leaf, Dusk Leaf is done in the late afternoon. Here you pick the dusk leaves.

flow.do: 1. Switch off the stove. 2. Put all four leaves in the small tumbler and cover them with spirit. 3. Stand the tumbler in a bowl of very hot water. 4. Wait 10 to 15 minutes, until the leaves are pale. 5. Meanwhile, mix 10 drops of iodine with about 50 drops of water in a cup. 6. Put one drop on some cooked rice.
flow.say: The spirit takes the green out, so that we can see the iodine change colour. Watch the spirit. What colour is it turning? What does iodine do on rice?
flow.kid: A grown-up warms the leaves in spirit. Watch the spirit turn green. Mix the iodine. Try one drop on rice.

ask.q: The spirit turned green. What has moved from the leaf into the spirit?
good: The green colour.
The chlorophyll has dissolved in the spirit.

flow.parent: Never heat spirit on a stove or near a flame. If the water cools before the leaves are pale, pour in fresh hot water. Thicker leaves can take 20 minutes. The rice turns blue-black, which shows your iodine works.
flow.context: This step of Dawn Leaf, Dusk Leaf takes the green colour out of the four leaves.

flow.do: 1. Lift the pale leaves out and rinse them in warm water. 2. Spread them flat on the white plate. 3. Cover them with the iodine mix and wait 3 minutes. 4. Rinse gently. 5. Give each leaf a score: 0 for yellow-brown, 1 for a few grey patches, 2 for grey-blue, 3 for dark blue, 4 for blue-black.
flow.say: Look closely before you say anything. Which leaves have snipped tips? What score would you give each leaf?
flow.kid: Rinse the leaves. Spread them on the plate. Pour on iodine. Wait 3 minutes. Give each leaf a score.
flow.parent: Most often the dusk leaves go dark blue or blue-black, and the dawn leaves stay much paler. If all four are dark, this plant does not empty their leaves in one night. Wrap a leaf in kitchen foil for two days and test it as a third kind. If all four stay brown, the plant had too little sun or stores little starch. Try another plant.
flow.context: This step of Dawn Leaf, Dusk Leaf is the iodine test on all four leaves.

flow.do: 1. Your child fills in the table. 2. Ask for the three sentences. 3. Ask where the starch went in the night. 4. Only then read the card 'How a leaf makes the day's starch last all night' together.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened. The dawn leaves had all night. So where did their starch go?
flow.kid: Fill in the table. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.

ask.q: Where did the dawn leaves' starch go during the night?
good: The plant used it for energy in the dark.
The leaf turned it into sugar and sent it to the roots and buds.

ask.q: Why did we test two leaves each time?
good: One leaf could be odd, such as a shaded or old leaf.
If both leaves agree, we can trust the result more.

check.q: In Dawn Leaf, Dusk Leaf, a leaf picked at sunrise stays pale with iodine. What is the best explanation?
options: Iodine does not work in the morning
The leaf never made any starch
The plant used up the starch during the night
check.why: The leaf made starch in yesterday's light. During the night the plant turned it back into sugar and used it, so little is left at sunrise. Choosing 'never made any' forgets that the dusk leaves from the same plant were full of starch.

flow.context: This is the last step of Dawn Leaf, Dusk Leaf. Here you explain your results.

experiments.title: The White Patch: does a leaf make starch where it is not green?
experiments.context: In this experiment you test a leaf that has green parts and white parts. You draw a map of the colours first, then do the iodine test. You will find out whether a leaf needs chlorophyll to make starch.
experiments.question: Does a leaf make starch in its white parts as well as its green parts? And what about a red or purple leaf?
experiments.predict: Guess first. After the iodine test, which parts of a green and white leaf will be blue-black: the green parts, the white parts, or all of the leaf? If you have a red leaf too, guess for that one. Write your guesses and the reason for each.
experiments.fair_test: The green and the white parts are on one leaf. So they had the same light, the same water and the same air. The only difference between them is the chlorophyll. Pick the leaf in the afternoon of a sunny day, when a leaf holds the most starch.

materials.item: one leaf with clear white or cream patches, from a plant that has stood in the sun. Variegated hibiscus, bougainvillea, snow bush and many coleus plants have such leaves. A neighbour or a nursery may give you one leaf.
one red or purple leaf, such as red amaranth or coleus (if you can get one)
surgical spirit or rubbing alcohol, enough to fill a small steel tumbler one third full. It catches fire easily.
povidone-iodine solution, the brown antiseptic sold at medical shops
a small steel tumbler, a big bowl, tongs or a spoon, and very hot water from a kettle or a pan
a white plate, a small cup, plain paper, a pencil and a green crayon

experiments.safety: Surgical spirit catches fire very easily. Never heat it on a stove or near a flame. Warm it only by standing its tumbler in hot water, with the stove switched off. Only a grown-up handles the hot water and the spirit. Iodine stains cloth and must not be swallowed.

schedule.what: On the afternoon of a sunny day: draw the leaf map, guess, do the iodine test and compare the leaf with the map.

experiments.record: Keep the leaf map. Beside it, put the leaf after the iodine test and take a photo, or draw it. Fill in the table. Then write what you thought, what you saw and why you think it happened.

setup.art: A green and white leaf lying on paper while a child traces round it and shades the green parts with a crayon.
setup.caption: 1. Trace the leaf and shade in the green parts. This is your map.

setup.art: A small steel tumbler holding the leaf in spirit, standing in a bowl of hot water, with a grown-up's hand holding tongs.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up dips the leaf in hot water, then warms it in spirit until it is pale.

setup.art: A pale leaf on a white plate with blue-black parts and yellow-brown parts, lying beside the crayon map.
setup.caption: 3. Cover the leaf with iodine. Compare it with your map.

flow.do: 1. Lay the leaf on paper and trace round it. 2. Draw the edges of the white patches. 3. Shade the green parts with the crayon. 4. Ask for the guess and the reason.
flow.say: This drawing is our map of where the chlorophyll is. Where do you think the starch will be? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Trace the leaf. Shade the green parts. Guess where the starch will be. Say why.
flow.parent: Patches that are yellow-green and not white still hold some chlorophyll. They may come out grey. Note them on the map as 'pale green'.
flow.context: This is the first step of the White Patch. Here you draw a map of the leaf and guess.

flow.do: 1. Switch off the stove. 2. A grown-up holds the leaf in just-boiled water for 1 minute. 3. Put it in the small tumbler and cover it with spirit. 4. Stand the tumbler in a bowl of very hot water for 10 to 15 minutes. 5. Do the same with the red leaf, if you have one. 6. Mix 10 drops of iodine with about 50 drops of water.
flow.say: Watch the red leaf in the hot water, and both leaves in the spirit. What colours come out, and into which liquid?
flow.kid: A grown-up dips the leaf in hot water. Then the leaf sits in warm spirit. Watch the colours.
flow.parent: Never heat spirit on a stove or near a flame. The red pigment of amaranth comes out in the hot water. The chlorophyll comes out in the spirit. Once the leaf is pale, the map is the only record of where the green was.
flow.context: This step of the White Patch takes the colour out of the leaf, so that the iodine can be seen.

flow.do: 1. Rinse the pale leaf in warm water and spread it on the white plate. 2. Cover it with the iodine mix and wait 3 minutes. 3. Rinse gently. 4. Lay it beside the map. 5. Fill in the table.
flow.say: Put the leaf next to your map. Which parts went blue-black? Do they match anything on the map?
flow.kid: Rinse the leaf. Pour on iodine. Wait 3 minutes. Put it beside your map. What matches?
flow.parent: The blue-black shape should match the shaded shape on the map closely. A red leaf usually goes blue-black all over, because red leaves have chlorophyll under the red.
flow.context: This step of the White Patch is the iodine test. Here you compare the tested leaf with your map.

flow.do: 1. Ask for the three sentences. 2. Ask how the white patch stays alive. 3. Only then read the card 'No chlorophyll, no starch' together.
flow.say: Say what you thought, what you saw and why. The white part makes no starch. So how does it stay alive?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw, and why. Then think about the white part.

ask.q: How does the white part of the leaf stay alive?
good: The green parts send sugar to it.
It lives on food made by the green cells next to it.

check.q: A green and white leaf had the same light all over. Only the green parts made starch. What does that show?
options: Iodine cannot stain white things
Starch is made only where there is chlorophyll
White parts get less sunlight
check.why: The light, water and air were the same for the whole leaf. The only difference was the chlorophyll, so chlorophyll is needed. Choosing 'less sunlight' forgets that both parts lie side by side in the same light. Iodine stains white rice well.

flow.context: This is the last step of the White Patch. Here you explain your result.

activities.title: Plate to Sun: follow your meal backwards
activities.context: In this activity you take a real meal and follow each food on it backwards, one living being at a time. You find out where every trail ends, and what nearly every trail has in common.

materials.item: today's lunch or dinner, or a list of what you ate yesterday
a large sheet of paper, a few small paper slips and a pencil

activities.record: Take a photo of your trails. Then write the one thing that nearly every trail passes through.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a circle for a plate in the middle and the names of five foods written inside it.
setup.caption: 1. Write each food on its own slip and lay the slips in a ring.

setup.art: The same sheet with arrows leading out from each food to a cow, a hen, a paddy plant and a fish, and on to grass and tiny sea algae.
setup.caption: 2. From each food, lay slips back along the trail: who made it, and what did they eat?

setup.art: The finished sheet with every trail ending at a small Sun in one corner, and salt and water circled with no trail.
setup.caption: 3. See where the trails end. Put aside anything with no trail.

flow.do: 1. Write each food of the meal on its own paper slip, with salt and water too. 2. Lay the slips in a ring on the big paper, like a plate. 3. Ask the opening question.
flow.say: Here is our meal. Is there one food here that did not need sunlight? Which one, and why do you think so?
flow.kid: Write each food on a slip. Lay them in a ring. Is there one that did not need sunlight? Say why.
flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children pick egg, fish, milk or mushroom.
flow.context: This is the first step of Plate to Sun. Here you draw your meal and make a guess.

flow.do: 1. Take one food at a time. 2. Ask who made it, and lay a slip with that living being next to it. 3. Ask what they ate, and add the next slip. 4. Go on until you reach a being who makes food from light. 5. Add a slip that says Sun.
flow.say: Who made this food? And what did they eat? Keep asking until you reach the Sun.
flow.kid: Pick one food. Who made it? What did they eat? Add slips until you reach the Sun.

ask.q: Who in the trail eats nothing at all?
good: The plant.
The plant makes food from air, water and light.
Tiny algae in the sea, for the fish.

flow.parent: For fish, the trail goes through tiny floating algae in the sea, not plants. For a mixed food such as sambar, one or two trails are enough.
flow.context: This is the main step of Plate to Sun. Here you draw the trail of each food.

flow.do: 1. Count how many trails end at the Sun. 2. Put aside anything that has no trail. 3. Ask what nearly every trail passed through just before the Sun.
flow.say: Where did the trails end? What is the last living being on each trail before the Sun? What do those beings share?
flow.kid: Count the trails that reach the Sun. Put aside anything with no trail. What comes just before the Sun?

check.q: A boiled egg is on your plate. Where does the egg's trail lead?
options: Hen, and it stops there
Straight to the Sun
Hen, then grain plants, then the Sun
check.why: The hen made the egg from the grain she ate, and the grain plants made the grain with sunlight. Stopping at the hen leaves out what the hen ate. The Sun cannot make an egg without a plant and a hen in between.

flow.context: This is the last step of Plate to Sun. Here you look at where all the trails end.

activities.title: The Banana Clock: watch starch turn into sugar
activities.context: In this activity you put iodine on slices of a raw banana, a just-ripe banana and a very ripe banana. You find out what a fruit does with its starch as it ripens.

materials.item: bananas at three stages: one green and raw (a cooking banana works), one just yellow, and one very ripe with brown spots
povidone-iodine solution, the brown antiseptic sold at medical shops
a white plate, a knife, a small cup and a notebook

activities.safety: Do not eat any slice that iodine has touched. Taste only clean slices. A grown-up cuts the raw banana, which is hard.
activities.record: Take a photo of the three slices after the iodine, or draw them. Under each, write how sweet a clean slice of that banana tasted, from 0 to 3.

setup.art: Three bananas in a row on a kitchen counter: one green, one yellow, one yellow with brown spots.
setup.caption: 1. Line up a raw banana, a just-ripe banana and a very ripe banana.

setup.art: Three round banana slices on a white plate with a drop of brown iodine being put on each.
setup.caption: 2. Cut one slice from each and cover it with iodine.

setup.art: The three slices after the test: one blue-black all over, one with a dark ring and a pale middle, and one almost all yellow-brown.
setup.caption: 3. Wait two minutes. Compare the three slices.

flow.do: 1. Cut two slices from each banana, about half a centimetre thick. 2. Put one slice of each on the plate, in order of ripeness. 3. Your child tastes the other three slices and gives each a sweetness score from 0 to 3. 4. Ask for a guess about the iodine.
flow.say: Taste each one. Which is sweetest? Now guess. Which slice will go darkest with iodine, and why?
flow.kid: Taste a clean slice of each. Score how sweet it is. Guess which slice will go darkest.
flow.parent: The raw banana tastes chalky and not sweet. That is safe to taste in a small bite.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Banana Clock. Here you taste the bananas and guess.

flow.do: 1. Mix 10 drops of iodine with about 50 drops of water in the cup. 2. Spoon the mix over the three slices on the plate. 3. Wait 2 minutes. 4. Your child puts the three slices in order, darkest first.
flow.say: Watch the three slices. Where does the dark colour show first? Is it the same all over each slice?
flow.kid: Pour iodine on the three slices. Wait 2 minutes. Put them in order, darkest first.
flow.parent: The raw slice goes blue-black all over. The just-ripe slice is patchy. The very ripe slice stays mostly yellow-brown. Throw the tested slices away.
flow.context: This is the main step of the Banana Clock. Here you do the iodine test on three slices.

flow.do: 1. Lay the sweetness scores beside the slices. 2. Ask what happened to the starch as the banana ripened. 3. Then read the card 'Sugar for now, starch for later, sucrose for travel'.
flow.say: The sweetest banana had the least starch. What do you think the banana did with the starch?
flow.kid: Compare sweetness with darkness. Where did the starch go as the banana got ripe?

ask.q: Wild bananas have seeds. Why would a fruit turn sweet when the seeds are ready?
good: A sweet fruit gets eaten.
The animal who eats the fruit carries the seeds away.

check.q: A raw banana goes blue-black with iodine, and a very ripe one hardly changes. Why?
options: The ripe banana turned starch into sugar
The ripe banana lost all its food
Iodine only works on green things
check.why: As a banana ripens, the fruit breaks starch chains into sugars. Sugar gives no colour with iodine, and it tastes sweet. The food is still there in a different form. Iodine works on white rice, so it does not need anything green.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Banana Clock. Here you link the starch to the sweetness.

activities.title: The Red Glow: what chlorophyll does with light in a jar
activities.context: In this activity you dissolve the chlorophyll from palak leaves in spirit. Then you shine a violet torch through the green liquid in a dark room, and see what the chlorophyll does with the light.

materials.item: fresh palak leaves, or any soft dark green leaves
surgical spirit or rubbing alcohol, enough to fill a small steel tumbler one third full. It catches fire easily.
a small ultraviolet torch of the kind sold for checking banknotes. A violet or blue LED light also works. A white torch gives only a faint glow.
two small clear glasses, a spoon, a steel bowl, a piece of clean cotton cloth, and water with a drop of green food colour or green watercolour paint

activities.safety: Surgical spirit catches fire easily, so keep it away from any flame, and let only a grown-up pour it. Never shine an ultraviolet torch into anyone's eyes. Do not drink the green liquid.
activities.record: Say what colour the beam was in each glass, or draw the glass in the dark and colour the beam. Write one sentence on what the chlorophyll did with the light.

setup.art: A child crushing torn palak leaves with the back of a spoon in a steel bowl with a little clear liquid.
setup.caption: 1. Tear the leaves. Crush them in spirit until the spirit is dark green.

setup.art: Green liquid being poured through a cotton cloth into a small clear glass.
setup.caption: 2. Strain the green liquid into a clear glass.

setup.art: A dark room with a small torch shining through the side of the glass, and the beam inside the green liquid glowing deep red.
setup.caption: 3. In a dark room, shine the violet torch through the glass. Look from the side.

flow.do: 1. Tear the leaves into small bits in the steel bowl. 2. A grown-up adds 4 tablespoons of spirit. 3. Crush the leaves hard with the back of the spoon for 3 minutes. 4. Strain the liquid through the cloth into a clear glass.
flow.say: We are taking the chlorophyll out of the leaves. We will use spirit, not water.
flow.kid: Tear the leaves. A grown-up adds spirit. Crush hard for 3 minutes. Strain the green liquid.

good: Chlorophyll dissolves in spirit.
It does not dissolve in water.

flow.parent: The liquid should be a clear dark green. If it is pale, crush more leaves into it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Red Glow. Here you take the chlorophyll out of palak leaves.

flow.do: 1. Put the glass of leaf liquid beside a glass of green coloured water. 2. Ask what colour each will show when violet light shines through it, and why. 3. Darken the room.
flow.say: Both liquids are green. We will shine violet light through each. What colour will we see in each glass? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Two green liquids. Guess what colour each shows in violet light. Say why.
flow.parent: Most people expect green or violet in both. Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: This step of the Red Glow is for guessing. You guess before you switch on the torch.

flow.do: 1. Shine the torch through the side of the leaf liquid and look from the side. 2. Do the same with the green coloured water. 3. Ask what your child saw. 4. Then read the card 'What happens when chlorophyll catches light' together.
flow.say: What colour is the beam inside the leaf liquid? And inside the coloured water? Where could the red light be coming from?
flow.kid: Shine the torch through each glass. Look from the side. What colour is each beam?
flow.parent: The beam in the leaf liquid glows a deep, dull red. The coloured water shows no red. Use the liquid on the same day, because chlorophyll in a glass breaks down in light.

check.q: Chlorophyll in a glass of spirit glows red in violet light. A living leaf hardly glows at all. Why?
options: The leaf has less chlorophyll than the glass
Living leaves catch no violet light
In the leaf, the caught energy is passed on and used
check.why: In a leaf, chlorophyll hands the caught energy on to be used for making sugar. In the glass it has nowhere to send the energy, so the energy comes back out as red light and heat. A leaf has plenty of chlorophyll, and it catches violet light well.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Red Glow. Here you shine violet light through the chlorophyll.

activities.title: Green Under Red: is there chlorophyll in a red leaf?
activities.context: In this activity you put red leaves in hot water and watch what happens to their colour. You find out whether a red leaf has chlorophyll.

materials.item: red amaranth leaves (red cheera, lal saag, sigappu keerai) from a vegetable shop. Red or purple coleus leaves also work.
a steel tumbler or a white cup, tongs or a spoon, and just-boiled water
a white plate

activities.safety: A grown-up pours the just-boiled water and lifts the leaves out.
activities.record: Lay the leaf you kept aside beside the leaf from the hot water and take a photo, or draw both. Write where each pigment went.

setup.art: Four red amaranth leaves on a white plate beside a cup of steaming water.
setup.caption: 1. Look at the red leaves. Keep one aside on the plate.

setup.art: Three leaves pushed under hot water in a white cup, with pink colour spreading into the water.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up puts three leaves in just-boiled water for five minutes.

setup.art: A dull green leaf lifted out on a spoon above a cup of pink-red water, with the untouched red leaf beside it for comparing.
setup.caption: 3. Lift a leaf out. Compare it with the leaf you kept aside.

flow.do: 1. Put four red leaves on the white plate and look at both sides. 2. Ask whether a red leaf has chlorophyll, and how we could find out. 3. Ask what hot water might do to the leaf.
flow.say: This leaf is red, not green. Does it have chlorophyll? What do you think, and why? How could we find out?
flow.kid: Look at the red leaves. Do they have chlorophyll? Say what you think and why.
flow.context: This is the first step of Green Under Red. Here you look at a red leaf and guess.

flow.do: 1. Keep one leaf aside. 2. A grown-up puts three leaves in the cup and pours just-boiled water over them. 3. Watch for 5 minutes.
flow.say: Watch the water and watch the leaves. What is changing? Tell me what you see, without explaining yet.
flow.kid: A grown-up pours hot water on three leaves. Watch the water. Watch the leaves. Say what you see.
flow.parent: The water turns pink, then red. The leaves turn dull green. This takes two to five minutes.
flow.context: This is the main step of Green Under Red. Here hot water takes one pigment out of the leaves.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up lifts one leaf out onto the plate. 2. Put it beside the leaf you kept aside. 3. Ask where the red went, and why the green stayed.
flow.say: Where is the red now? Where is the green? One pigment went into the water and one did not. What does that tell you about each?
flow.kid: Compare the two leaves. Look at the colour of each one.

ask.q: Why did the red leave and the green stay?
good: The red pigment dissolves in water.
Chlorophyll does not dissolve in water. It needs spirit.

check.q: Hot water turns pink and a red amaranth leaf turns green. What does this show?
options: The leaf had chlorophyll all along, under the red
Hot water makes new chlorophyll
The red pigment turned into green pigment
check.why: The red pigment dissolved in the water and left the leaf. The chlorophyll does not dissolve in water, so it stayed and could now be seen. Hot water kills the leaf cells, so nothing new is made.

flow.context: This is the last step of Green Under Red. Here you work out where each pigment went.

activities.title: Measure the Sun Catcher: how much leaf does one plant hold out?
activities.context: In this activity you measure the area of a few leaves on squared paper. Then you work out the area of all the leaves on one potted plant, and compare it with the area of the pot. You will find out how many times more leaf than pot a plant holds out to the light.

materials.item: a potted plant with fewer than about 60 leaves
squared paper with 1 centimetre squares, such as a page from a maths notebook. If the squares are smaller, rule your own 1 centimetre lines.
a pencil and a ruler

activities.record: Keep the leaf outlines with the square counts written inside. Write the total leaf area, the area of the top of the pot, and how many times bigger the leaf area is.

setup.art: A child holding a leaf, still on the plant, flat against squared paper and drawing round it with a pencil.
setup.caption: 1. Trace a small, a middle and a big leaf on squared paper. Do not pick them.

setup.art: A leaf outline on squared paper with the whole squares ticked and the part squares marked.
setup.caption: 2. Count the squares inside each outline.

setup.art: A notebook page with a sum: mean leaf area times number of leaves, beside a drawing of the pot seen from above with its width measured.
setup.caption: 3. Multiply by the number of leaves. Compare with the top of the pot.

flow.do: 1. Look at the plant from directly above. 2. Ask whether all the leaves together are bigger or smaller than the top of the pot, and why. 3. Count the leaves and write the number.
flow.say: Look down on the plant. If we laid all the leaves flat, side by side, would they cover more than the pot or less? Why?
flow.kid: Look down on the plant. Guess: do the leaves cover more than the pot? Count the leaves.
flow.context: This is the first step of Measure the Sun Catcher. Here you guess and count the leaves.

flow.do: 1. Choose a small, a middle and a big leaf. 2. Hold each one flat on the squared paper, still on the plant, and trace round it. 3. Count the whole squares inside. 4. Count a part square as 1 if it is half or more, and as 0 if it is less. 5. Add the three areas and divide by 3.
flow.say: Each square is one square centimetre. Count the squares inside each outline. The mean is the three areas added up, then divided by 3.
flow.kid: Trace three leaves. Count the squares in each. Add the three numbers. Divide by 3.
flow.parent: Counting part squares this way is an estimate, and that is fine. The mean of a small, a middle and a big leaf stands for all the leaves.
flow.context: This is the main step of Measure the Sun Catcher. Here you measure three leaves on squared paper.

flow.do: 1. Multiply the mean leaf area by the number of leaves. 2. Measure the top of the pot. For a round pot, multiply the width by itself and take three quarters. 3. Divide the leaf area by the pot area. 4. Ask why a plant holds out so much leaf.
flow.say: How many times bigger is the leaf area than the pot? Why would a plant spread out so much flat green surface?
flow.kid: Multiply the mean by the number of leaves. Work out the pot's area. How many times bigger?
flow.parent: Width times width times three quarters is close enough for a circle. Most healthy pot plants hold out between 2 and 6 times the area of their pot.

check.q: Why do most leaves grow thin and flat, not thick and round?
options: Round leaves cannot be green
A flat leaf catches more light for the same material
A flat leaf is heavier
check.why: Light is caught only at a surface that faces it. A thin, flat leaf spreads its chloroplasts over a wide area, so more of them get light. A ball of the same material would hide most of its cells in its own shade.

flow.context: This is the last step of Measure the Sun Catcher. Here you compare the leaf area with the pot.

activities.title: A Photon's Journey: draw the comic strip
activities.context: In this activity you draw a comic strip of six boxes. It follows the energy of one photon from the Sun, through a leaf, into starch, through the night, and into someone's meal.

materials.item: a sheet of plain paper, a ruler, a pencil and colour pencils

activities.record: Keep the comic strip. Read it aloud to someone who has not done this lesson, and see whether they can follow it.

setup.art: A sheet of paper ruled into six boxes, with the first box showing the Sun and a small dot of light leaving it.
setup.caption: 1. Rule six boxes. Start with a photon leaving the Sun.

setup.art: The middle boxes showing the dot of light landing on a leaf, a chlorophyll molecule catching it, and a starch grain forming.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the catch, the sugar and the starch.

setup.art: The last boxes showing a leaf at night sending sugar down to a root, and a child eating tapioca.
setup.caption: 3. Draw the night, and the meal at the end.

flow.do: 1. Rule the paper into six boxes. 2. Ask your child to tell the journey aloud first, in their own words. 3. Write six short titles together, one for each box.
flow.say: A photon is one tiny packet of light. Tell me the journey first. A photon leaves the Sun. What happens to its energy, step by step, until someone eats it?
flow.kid: Rule six boxes. Tell the journey aloud first. Write a short title in each box.
flow.parent: One good plan: 1 leaving the Sun, 2 caught by chlorophyll, 3 sugar is built, 4 stored as starch at dusk, 5 sent as sucrose at night, 6 eaten.
flow.context: This is the first step of A Photon's Journey. Here you plan the six boxes of the comic.

flow.do: 1. Your child makes the six boxes. They draw each one. Or they lay out small things in it, such as a torch for the Sun, a leaf, or a bean for starch. 2. In box 2, they show what they think happens inside the chloroplast, including what cannot be seen. 3. They add one sentence under each box.
flow.say: Show what you think happens, even the parts nobody can see. A drawing or an arrangement that explains an idea is called a model.
flow.kid: Make all six boxes, by drawing or with small things. Show the parts nobody can see too. Write one sentence under each.
flow.context: This is the main step of A Photon's Journey. Here you draw the comic strip.

flow.do: 1. Your child reads the strip aloud. 2. Ask where the energy is in each box. 3. Ask what happens to the photon itself.
flow.say: In each box, where is the energy now? And is the photon still there after box 2?
flow.kid: Read your comic aloud. Point to where the energy is in each box.

check.q: A chlorophyll molecule catches a photon. What happens to the photon?
options: It turns into a grain of starch
It is gone, and its energy is now in an electron
It stays inside the leaf as light
check.why: A photon is a packet of energy. When it is caught, the photon no longer exists, and an electron in the chlorophyll holds its energy. Light is not stored as light. Starch is made of atoms from air and water, and the photon's energy only helped to join them.

flow.context: This is the last step of A Photon's Journey. Here you check the comic by following the energy.

projects.title: Leaf Prints That Fade: what light does to chlorophyll outside a leaf
projects.context: In this five-day project you make green prints on paper by rubbing fresh leaves. You keep half of each print covered and put one print in the sun. You find out what light does to chlorophyll that is no longer in a living leaf.

materials.item: fresh soft green leaves, such as palak, tulsi, hibiscus or any soft garden weed
sheets of thick white paper
a steel spoon
black paper or thick cardboard, and paper clips or tape

schedule.what: Make two leaf prints. Cover half of each. Put one at a sunny window and one in a closed drawer.
Lift the covers for a moment and look. Put them back.
Take off the covers. Compare all four halves and explain.

projects.record: On day 1, day 3 and day 5, write the colour of each of the four halves: sun and open, sun and covered, drawer and open, drawer and covered. On day 5 write which half changed most, and why you think so.

setup.art: A leaf folded inside a sheet of white paper while a child rubs hard over it with the back of a steel spoon.
setup.caption: 1. Fold a leaf inside the paper. Rub hard with a spoon until green shows through.

setup.art: Two sheets each showing a green leaf-shaped print, with a strip of black paper clipped over the left half of each.
setup.caption: 2. Make two prints. Cover half of each with black paper.

setup.art: One print taped inside a sunny window and the other being put into a drawer.
setup.caption: 3. Put one at a sunny window and one in a drawer. Wait five days.

flow.do: 1. Fold a sheet of paper in half with two or three leaves inside. 2. Rub hard all over with the back of the spoon, until the paper is stained green. 3. Open it and peel off the leaf bits. 4. Make a second print the same way and let both dry. 5. Clip black paper over half of each print. 6. Put one at a sunny window and one in a drawer. 7. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: The green on the paper is chlorophyll, out of its leaf. What will five days of sunlight do to it? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Rub leaves inside folded paper. Make two green prints. Cover half of each. Guess what the sun will do.
flow.parent: Soft, juicy leaves give the darkest print. There are four halves to compare: sun and open, sun and covered, drawer and open, drawer and covered.
flow.context: This is day 1 of Leaf Prints That Fade. Here you make two prints and set them up.

flow.do: 1. Lift each cover for a moment. 2. Compare the open half with the covered half. 3. Write down what you see. 4. Put the covers back in the same place.
flow.say: Is there any difference yet between the two halves at the window? And in the drawer?
flow.kid: Lift the covers. Compare the halves. Write what you see. Put the covers back.
flow.context: This is day 3 of Leaf Prints That Fade. Here you take a first look.

flow.do: 1. Take off both covers. 2. Lay the two prints side by side. 3. Your child says which half changed most. 4. Ask why a living leaf in the same window stays green.
flow.say: Which half faded most? A leaf on a plant sits in the sun for months and stays green. So what is different about a living leaf?
flow.kid: Take off the covers. Lay the prints side by side. Which half faded most?

ask.q: Why does a living leaf stay green in the same sunlight?
good: The leaf passes the light's energy on and uses it.
The living leaf mends and replaces what the light harms.

flow.parent: The open half at the window usually fades to yellow-brown. The covered half and the drawer print stay greener. If you see little change, leave the print for three more sunny days. In a living leaf, parts harmed by bright light are replaced all day long, some of them about every half hour.

check.q: A green leaf print fades in the sun, but a living leaf in the same sun stays green. Why?
options: A living leaf catches less light than paper
Paper takes the green colour out
A living leaf uses the energy and replaces harmed parts
check.why: On paper, chlorophyll catches light and has nowhere to send the energy. The energy harms the chlorophyll, and nothing replaces it. A living leaf passes the energy on and keeps mending. The covered half of the print stayed green on the same paper, so the paper is not the cause.

flow.context: This is day 5 of Leaf Prints That Fade. Here you compare the four halves and explain.

challenges.title: The Leaf Tower: fix 12 leaves on one stem so that none is in the shade
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. A leaf in the shade of another leaf catches little light. Here you fix twelve paper leaves on one stem so that a lamp above can reach as many of them as possible.
challenges.problem: Fix 12 paper leaves onto one upright stick. Seen from directly above, as many leaves as possible must be fully in view. A leaf that is hidden under another leaf is in the shade.
constraints: The stem is one stick, about 30 centimetres tall. No extra branches.
Every leaf is 4 centimetres wide and 6 centimetres long, on a stalk no longer than 4 centimetres.
All 12 leaves must be fixed to the stem, and no two leaves may be fixed at the same height.
materials: a straight stick, a pencil or a drinking straw about 30 centimetres long
a lump of atta dough or a cup of uncooked rice to hold the stick upright
green or plain paper, scissors and sticky tape
12 toothpicks, broomstick bits or strips of thin card for the leaf stalks
a phone camera, or a chair to stand on with a grown-up beside you
general: Fix the leaves in two rows, on opposite sides of the stem.
Make the lower stalks longer than the upper ones.
Tilt each leaf a little, so that it does not lie right under the one above.
creative: Go round the stem in a spiral, turning each leaf a little further than the last, as a sunflower plant does.
Fix the leaves in pairs, and turn each pair a quarter turn from the pair below, as a tulsi plant does.
Make each leaf point a little downward, so that light slips past it to the leaf below.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own leaf tower. Plan it on paper or with loose leaves, build it and score it from above. Then move the lamp to one side, as the Sun is in the morning, and score it again from where the lamp is. Which design was best for both?

setup.art: A stick standing upright in a lump of dough, with twelve cut-out paper leaves on toothpick stalks lying beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Stand the stick up. Cut 12 paper leaves and tape each to a stalk.

setup.art: A paper leaf tower seen from the side, with leaves going round the stick in a spiral.
setup.caption: 2. Fix all 12 leaves to the stem, each at a different height.

setup.art: The same tower photographed from directly above, showing how many leaves are in full view.
setup.caption: 3. Look straight down from above. Count the leaves you can see fully.

flow.do: 1. Stand the stick in the dough. 2. Cut 12 paper leaves, each 4 by 6 centimetres. 3. Tape each leaf to a stalk. 4. Fix all 12 in one straight row up one side of the stem. 5. Look from directly above, or take a photo from above. 6. Score 2 for each leaf fully in view, 1 for a leaf partly hidden, 0 for a hidden leaf.
flow.say: First we need a score to beat. All the leaves are in one row. From above, how many can you see fully?
flow.kid: Fix 12 leaves in one straight row. Look from above. Score 2, 1 or 0 for each leaf.
flow.parent: A single row scores very low, because the top leaf hides most of the others. The best possible score is 24.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Leaf Tower. Here you build a poor design and score it.

flow.do: 1. Look at the usual ideas together. 2. Your child chooses one and says why it should work. 3. They rebuild the tower and score it from above.
flow.say: Which idea do you think will let the most light through to the lower leaves? Why? Build it and score it.
flow.kid: Pick one idea. Say why it should work. Rebuild the tower. Score it from above.

ask.q: Why do longer stalks on the lower leaves help?
good: The lower leaves reach out beyond the shade of the upper ones.

flow.context: This step of the Leaf Tower tests one of the usual ideas.

flow.do: 1. Your child plans a tower of their own, on paper or by laying the loose leaves out as seen from above. 2. They build it and score it. 3. Move the lamp, or your eye, to one side and score it again. 4. Look at a real plant from above and compare.
flow.say: Now design your own. What will you change, and why? Then look down on a real plant. What has the plant done about shade?
flow.kid: Design your own tower. Plan it on paper or with loose leaves. Build it. Score it. Then look down on a real plant.
flow.parent: Look down on a tulsi, a hibiscus or a papaya plant from above. You will see very little overlap between the leaves.

check.q: Seen from above, the leaves of many plants hardly overlap. What does this do for the plant?
options: Each leaf gets light, so more food is made
It keeps the leaves dry in the rain
It makes the plant taller
check.why: A leaf under another leaf gets little light and makes little food, but still costs material to build. A plant whose leaves hardly overlap gets more light for the same number of leaves.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Leaf Tower. Here you build your own design and compare it with a real plant.

items.p: What does chlorophyll do in a leaf?
items.why: Chlorophyll is the pigment that catches light. Choosing 'joins sugar into starch' mixes up the catcher with the builders. Enzymes do the building.

items.p: True or false: chlorophyll is spread evenly through every part of a leaf cell.
items.why: False. Chlorophyll sits only inside the chloroplasts, the small green bodies in the cell. The rest of the cell has no colour.

items.p: Brown iodine solution turns ____ where it touches starch.
items.why: Iodine particles slip inside the coiled starch chain, and the two together look blue-black. 'Dark blue' or 'black' are also right.

items.p: Put the steps of the starch test on a leaf in order.
a: Dip the leaf in very hot water
Warm the leaf in spirit until pale
Rinse the leaf in warm water
items.why: Hot water kills the cells and lets liquids in. Spirit takes out the green. The rinse softens the leaf. Iodine then shows the starch.
items: Rinse the leaf in warm water
Warm the leaf in spirit until pale
Dip the leaf in very hot water

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
items.why: These words are used all through the unit. A strong answer could give an example of each.
pairs: the green pigment that catches light
the tiny green body where photosynthesis happens
a long chain of glucose that stores food
the sugar that travels inside a plant
a living being who makes their own food

items.p: Leaves are picked from one plant at sunrise and at sunset. Which usually go darker with iodine?
items.why: A leaf builds up starch through the day, so it holds the most at sunset. Choosing 'both the same' usually comes from how the leaves look. Starch cannot be seen without the test.

items.p: In Dawn Leaf, Dusk Leaf, you test two leaves from each time of day. Why not one?
items.a: One leaf can be odd. It may have been shaded, old or damaged. If two leaves from the same time agree, the result can be trusted more.
items.why: A strong answer says that a single result can be a fluke, and that a repeat checks it.

items.p: Sort these living beings into producers and consumers.
items.why: Plants, algae and cyanobacteria make food from light, so they are producers. Animals, including humans, eat food that was made by others.

items.p: Draw a green and white leaf after the iodine test. Label the parts with starch and without.
items.a: A leaf outline with the parts that were green coloured blue-black and labelled 'starch', and the parts that were white coloured yellow-brown and labelled 'no starch'.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the blue-black exactly where the green was. Colouring the whole leaf dark shows the idea that light alone is enough.
items.art: A blank leaf outline with a wavy inner line dividing the middle from the edge.

items.p: True or false: a red amaranth leaf has no chlorophyll.
items.why: False. The chlorophyll is under the red pigment. Hot water takes out the red, and the leaf turns green.

items.p: Why is the leaf warmed in spirit during the starch test?
opts: To take the green colour out
To add starch to the leaf
To kill germs on the leaf
items.why: Chlorophyll dissolves in spirit. With the green gone, the blue-black of the iodine is easy to see. Spirit adds nothing to the leaf.

items.p: The sugar that travels through a plant's phloem is called ____.
items.why: Sucrose is the travelling sugar. It is the same sugar as kitchen sugar. Glucose is made first, and starch is the stored form.

items.p: Three of these hold energy that a plant caught from sunlight. Which one does not?
items.why: Rice, jaggery and coconut oil were all made by plants using sunlight. Salt is a mineral from sea water or rock, and gives no energy.

items.p: Follow a bowl of curd back to the Sun. Name each living being on the way.
items.a: Curd bacteria turned milk into curd. A cow made the milk. The cow ate grass. The grass made food from sunlight.
items.why: A strong answer names all three living beings in order and ends at a plant catching light.

items.p: Draw a plant with leaves, a fruit and a root. Label where sugar is made, travels and is stored.
a: Travels: through the phloem in the stem
Stored: in the fruit and the root
items.why: Sugar is made only in green parts. It travels as sucrose and is stored again, often as starch. Seeds and stems are also right for 'stored'.
items.art: A simple plant with three leaves, one fruit and a fat root, and three blank label lines.

items.p: A white patch on a leaf makes no food. How do its cells stay alive?
opts: Green cells nearby send them sugar
They take food from the soil
items.why: Sucrose flows from the green cells to the white ones. Choosing 'from the soil' is an old idea about plants. Soil gives water and minerals, not food.

worksheets.title: Light, starch and who feeds whom (stretch)

items.p: Which colours of light does chlorophyll take in most?
items.why: Chlorophyll takes in mostly red and blue light. Choosing 'green' is a common mix-up. Green is the colour a leaf sends back most, which is why we see it.

items.p: Explain why a leaf looks green.
items.a: Chlorophyll takes in mostly red and blue light. More of the green light is sent back or passes through, and that green light reaches our eyes.
items.why: A strong answer says the colour we see is the light the leaf does not keep. An answer such as 'because it uses green light' has it the wrong way round.

items.p: True or false: a leaf catches no green light at all.
items.why: False. A leaf catches a good part of the green light too, only less than the red and the blue.

items.p: A leaf holds 60 units of starch at dusk. The night is 12 hours. How many units an hour last until dawn?
items.why: 60 ÷ 12 = 5. At 5 units an hour the starch lasts exactly 12 hours.

items.p: Scientists made night come four hours early for thale cress plants. What did the plants do?
items.why: The plants slowed down at once, and the starch still lasted until dawn. A plant makes no starch in the dark, because photosynthesis needs light.

items.p: Every chlorophyll molecule has one atom of ____ at its centre.
items.why: Magnesium sits in the middle of the chlorophyll molecule. A plant short of magnesium turns yellow.

items.p: Sort these by how the plant mainly stores food in them.
items.why: All of this food arrived as sucrose from the leaves. Each part then stores it in its own way. An iodine test would turn only the starch group blue-black.

items.p: Put this food chain in order, starting with the producer.
items.why: The algae catch sunlight. Tiny animals eat the algae, the sardine eats them, and the child eats the sardine.

items.p: Three people talk about who makes a plant's food.
items.a: A strong answer uses evidence: the white patch for the textbook, a food chain for the physicist, or the Red Glow for the plant scientist. It also gives a fair point to another view.
items.why: Each is right about one part. Chlorophyll is needed, the energy is the Sun's, and only the whole chloroplast can turn that energy into sugar.

views.says: Chlorophyll makes the food. No chlorophyll, no food.
The Sun makes the food. All the energy in it comes from sunlight.
The whole living leaf makes the food. Chlorophyll alone in a jar makes nothing.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with most? Use one test from this lesson as evidence. Then say what one of the others has right.

items.p: In the Banana Clock, the very ripe slice hardly changed colour with iodine. Why?
opts: Its food had been used up
Its starch had turned into sugar
items.why: A ripening banana breaks starch into sugars, and sugar gives no colour with iodine. The food is still there, as sugar.

items.p: Draw what happens to a photon's energy in a leaf, and in a jar of chlorophyll. Use two boxes.
items.a: Box 1: a photon lands on chlorophyll in a leaf, and an arrow leads on to 'sugar'. Box 2: a photon lands on chlorophyll in a jar, and arrows lead back out as 'red light' and 'heat'.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the energy being passed on in the leaf and coming straight back out in the jar.
items.art: Two empty boxes side by side, one with a small leaf in the corner and one with a small glass in the corner.

items.p: True or false: plants store starch because starch dissolves easily in water.
items.why: False. Starch does not dissolve. That is why it is good for storing. It sits in the cell as small grains and does not pull water in.

items.p: Three of these photosynthesise. Which one does not?
items.why: A mushroom is a fungus with no chlorophyll, and feeds on dead plants. Seaweed, cyanobacteria and paddy all make food from light.

items.p: A pure white seedling grows well for three weeks and then dies. Explain both parts.
items.a: For three weeks the seedling lives on food stored in the seed. With no chlorophyll they catch no light and make no new food. When the seed is empty, they starve.
items.why: A strong answer explains the good start by the seed's store, and the death by the missing chlorophyll.

items.p: Match each living being to the way they are fed.
items.why: Only the hibiscus and the coral's algae catch light themselves. The others live on food that someone else made.
pairs: takes sucrose from a green plant
fed by bacteria that use chemicals
fed by algae living inside their body

items.p: List the four liquids used in the starch test on a leaf. Beside each, write its job.
a: Very hot water: kills the cells and lets liquids in
Warm spirit: takes out the chlorophyll
Warm rinse water: softens the leaf
items.why: Each step does one job. Skipping the hot water or the spirit gives a result that is hard to read.
items.art: Four empty tumblers in a row with a blank label line under each.

items.p: People say 'the energy is in the sugar'. What is the more exact way to say it?
items.a: The energy is in sugar and oxygen kept apart. It comes out when the two react and turn back into carbon dioxide and water.
items.why: A strong answer brings in the oxygen. Sugar gives energy only when it reacts with oxygen, in a flame or in a cell.

items.p: Most bacteria at deep-sea hot springs still need one thing that photosynthesis made. What is it?
items.why: They use oxygen to get energy from hydrogen sulphide. That oxygen was made by algae and plants far above, and was carried down in the sea water.

items.p: A square metre of paddy gives 300 grams of rice. You eat 150 grams a day. How many days does it last?
items.why: 300 ÷ 150 = 2. One square metre of field feeds you rice for only two days.

items.p: True or false: every living being on Earth depends on sunlight.
items.why: False. Some microbes deep inside rock live on hydrogen made by natural radioactivity. So the true word is 'almost every'.

items.p: Two groups of scientists talk about a leaf's starch at night.
items.a: A strong answer sees that both explain the same results, and suggests a test where the two would differ, such as changing the sugar level without changing the starch.
items.why: This is a real, open argument. A good scientist can say what would change their mind.

views.says: The plant measures the starch and the hours left, and divides one by the other.
No division is needed. Sugar levels shift the plant's daily clock, and the clock sets the speed.

items.ask: Both agree on what the plant does. They disagree on how. What test could help to choose between them? Which do you find more likely, and why?

items.p: How do satellites measure photosynthesis from space?
opts: By the faint red glow of leaves
items.why: Chlorophyll in living leaves gives off a very faint red glow while it works. Satellites have measured this glow over the whole Earth since 2011.

items.p: Making food with energy from chemicals, not from light, is called ____.
items.why: Chemo means 'chemical' and photo means 'light'. Some bacteria make food by chemosynthesis.

items.p: You wrap one tulsi leaf in foil for two days. Plan a fair starch test. What do you compare it with?
items.a: Test the wrapped leaf together with an unwrapped leaf of the same size from the same plant, picked at the same time. Use the same spirit and iodine for both.
items.why: A strong answer names the comparison leaf and keeps everything else the same. Without the second leaf, a pale result could mean the test failed.

items.p: Put in order what happens to light energy in a leaf.
a: The energy reaches a reaction centre
items.why: The light is caught first. The energy is passed on, then used to build sugar, and part of the sugar is stored as starch.
items: The energy reaches a reaction centre

items.p: A plant short of magnesium turns yellow. Why?
items.why: Every chlorophyll molecule needs one magnesium atom. With too little magnesium, less chlorophyll is made, and the yellow pigments show.

items.p: Sketch a line graph of the starch in a leaf over 24 hours, from sunrise to the next sunrise.
items.a: A line that starts low at sunrise, rises through the day to a peak at sunset, then falls in a straight line through the night to nearly zero at the next sunrise.
items.why: A strong sketch shows a steady fall at night, not a sudden drop. The line should reach almost zero at dawn, not hours before.
items.art: Empty graph axes labelled 'time of day' along the bottom and 'starch in the leaf' up the side, with sunrise, sunset and sunrise marked.

items.p: Three of these need oxygen made by photosynthesis. Which one does not?
items.why: Fish, children and most hot spring bacteria use oxygen that photosynthesis made. The microbes deep in rock use hydrogen and need no oxygen.

items.p: Name one thing about chlorophyll or starch that scientists still argue about.
items.a: One answer: how a plant sets the speed of starch use at night. Another: whether green sea slugs really live on the chloroplasts they take from algae.
items.why: Any open question from this lesson is right, as long as it is truly unsettled.

items.p: True or false: chlorophyll on paper fades in sunlight, but chlorophyll in a living leaf is kept in repair.
items.why: True. A living leaf passes the caught energy on and replaces harmed parts all day. On paper nothing replaces them.

items.p: Sort these into 'settled' and 'still argued about'.
items.why: Science has both kinds of statement. Saying which is which is part of being honest about what we know.
items: Leaves use up most of their starch by dawn
Plants do division to share out starch
A green sea slug lives on sunlight
The sea does about half of all photosynthesis
Life began at deep-sea hot springs

items.p: Of 1,000 units of sunlight energy on a field, the crop stores about 10. What share is that?
items.why: 10 out of 1,000 is the same as 1 out of 100. Most of the light warms the field, passes through or is sent back.

quiz.p: Where in a leaf cell is the chlorophyll?
quiz.why: Chlorophyll sits in thin skins inside the chloroplasts. Choosing 'dissolved in the water' is a fair guess, but chlorophyll does not dissolve in water.

quiz.p: A chlorophyll molecule catches a photon. What happens first?
quiz.why: The photon's energy lifts an electron in the chlorophyll. Sugar and starch come later, after the energy is passed on.

quiz.p: In the starch test, what is the job of the very hot water?
opts: It kills the cells and lets liquids in
quiz.why: Hot water stops the cells using starch and breaks their thin skins. Taking the green out is the job of the spirit.

quiz.p: When does a leaf on a sunny balcony hold the most starch?
quiz.why: Starch builds up all day and is used up all night. So it is highest late in the afternoon and lowest just before sunrise.

quiz.p: A green and white leaf is tested with iodine. Which parts turn blue-black?
opts: Only the parts that were green
Only the parts that were white
quiz.why: Starch is made only where there is chlorophyll. Choosing 'the whole leaf' usually means thinking that light alone is enough.

quiz.p: A purple coleus leaf turns blue-black in the starch test. What does that show?
opts: It has chlorophyll under the purple
quiz.why: Starch needs chlorophyll. So the leaf must have chlorophyll, hidden by the purple pigment.

quiz.p: How does food made in a tapioca leaf reach the root?
opts: It is made in the root
As starch grains, through the soil
quiz.why: Starch does not dissolve, so it cannot travel. The leaf turns it into sucrose, which flows through the phloem. The root then stores it as starch again.

quiz.p: Why does a leaf store food as starch and not as dissolved sugar?
opts: Starch does not dissolve or pull in water
quiz.why: A lot of dissolved sugar would draw water into the cell and swell it. Starch sits as small grains and causes no such trouble.

quiz.p: True or false: the fish in a fish curry needed sunlight.
quiz.why: True. The fish ate smaller animals, who ate tiny sea algae, and the algae made food from sunlight.

quiz.p: What comes first in nearly every food chain?
quiz.why: Nearly every chain begins with a plant, an alga or a cyanobacterium making food from light. Soil gives minerals and water, not energy.

quiz.p: What feeds the giant tubeworms at hot springs on the deep sea floor?
opts: Bacteria that use chemicals for energy
quiz.why: No light reaches the deep sea floor, so no seaweed grows there. Bacteria inside the tubeworms make food using energy from chemicals in the hot water.

quiz.p: Which of these do scientists still argue about?
opts: How a plant sets the speed of starch use at night
quiz.why: Everyone agrees that leaves use starch at a steady rate that lasts until dawn. How the plant sets that rate is not settled.

applications: Farmers and gardeners check leaf colour to see whether a crop needs more nitrogen. Paler leaves have less chlorophyll. Many paddy farmers in India hold a printed colour card against the leaf to decide.
Apple growers use the iodine test on a cut apple to decide when to harvest. Less blue-black means more starch has turned into sugar.
Satellites measure the faint red glow of chlorophyll to watch crops, forests and droughts across whole countries.
Sago, cornflour and the starch used to stiffen cotton saris are all plant starch, washed out of tapioca roots, maize grains or rice.
Hay and green fodder cut in the afternoon hold more sugar and starch than fodder cut at dawn. Some farmers time their cutting by this.
Scientists are trying to copy chlorophyll's light catching in 'artificial leaves' that would make fuel from sunlight, water and carbon dioxide. None is cheap and long-lasting yet.
Sugar mills and jaggery makers collect the sucrose that sugarcane leaves made and sent down to the stem.

open_questions.q: How does a plant set the speed at which they use starch at night?
open_questions.why_open: The steady rate has been measured many times. Scientists have at least two different explanations for how the plant does it, and the chemicals involved have not all been found.

open_questions.q: Do all plants share out their night food in the same way as thale cress?
open_questions.why_open: Most of the careful work was done on one small plant in laboratories. Rice and wheat store more sugar and less starch in their leaves, and far less is known about them.

open_questions.q: Does the green sea slug really live on the chloroplasts taken from algae?
open_questions.why_open: The stolen chloroplasts keep working for months. But related slugs lived just as long in the dark, so the chloroplasts may be mainly a food store.

open_questions.q: Did life on Earth begin with chemosynthesis at deep-sea hot springs, before any living being could use light?
open_questions.why_open: The oldest traces of life are hard to read, and nobody has yet made a living cell from chemicals in a laboratory.

open_questions.q: Why did life settle on chlorophyll, which leaves much of the green light uncaught?
open_questions.why_open: There are several ideas. One is that catching every colour would make the energy supply too jumpy to handle safely. None has been proved.

ask_kids: Which plant caught the sunlight for this food, and about when?
This leaf looks the same as it did this morning. What might have changed inside it since then?
If you had chlorophyll in your skin, could you skip lunch? What else would you need?
Why is a raw banana not sweet and a ripe one sweet?
Is there anything on this plate that never needed the Sun?
Why do you think plants are flat and spread out, and animals are lumpy and move about?
Where does a tree's trunk get food from, when it has no leaves of its own?
The plant on our balcony got through last night without making any food. How?

jokes.j: Why did the leaf open a bank account?
jokes.a: To save some starch for the night!

jokes.j: What did the white patch say to the green patch?
Why did the iodine turn blue-black?
jokes.a: It met some starch and got all wound up!

maths.problem: In Dawn Leaf, Dusk Leaf, the two dusk leaves scored 4 and 3 for starch. The two dawn leaves scored 1 and 0. What is the mean score for each time? What is the difference?
maths.explain: Dusk: 4 + 3 = 7, and 7 ÷ 2 = 3.5. Dawn: 1 + 0 = 1, and 1 ÷ 2 = 0.5. Then 3.5 − 0.5 = 3. So the dusk leaves scored 3 points higher on a scale of 4.
maths.context: This is about Dawn Leaf, Dusk Leaf. You test leaves picked at sunrise and at sunset for starch, and give each a score from 0 to 4.
maths.why_maths: Two leaves from the same time rarely score exactly the same. The mean gives one fair number for each time, so that you can compare them.

maths.problem: A leaf holds 60 units of starch at dusk. The night is 12 hours long. What steady rate uses it all exactly by dawn? In December the night is 15 hours. What rate is needed now?
maths.answer: 5 units an hour for the 12-hour night. 4 units an hour for the 15-hour night.
maths.explain: 60 ÷ 12 = 5. For the longer night, 60 ÷ 15 = 4. A longer night means the same starch must be spread more thinly, so the plant has less to grow on each hour.
maths.context: This is about how a leaf uses starch at night. In Dawn Leaf, Dusk Leaf you saw that a leaf is full of starch at dusk and nearly empty at dawn.
maths.why_maths: Sharing a store equally over a number of hours is division. It shows why the plant must use starch more slowly on a long night.

maths.problem: In the Starch Bank game you have 14 beans. You choose to spend 4 in each part of the night. Then the card says the night has 5 parts. Do your beans last? What is the biggest number you could safely have chosen?
maths.answer: No. The beans run out during the fourth part. The biggest safe number was 2.
maths.explain: 4 beans in each of 5 parts needs 4 × 5 = 20 beans, and you have 14. After 3 parts you have spent 12, and only 2 are left for the fourth. For a safe number, divide: 14 ÷ 5 = 2 with 4 left over. So 2 in each part is safe, and 3 is not, because 3 × 5 = 15.
maths.context: This is about the Starch Bank game. You collect beans by day and must share them out equally over the parts of the night.
maths.why_maths: Checking a plan before you carry it out saves the plant from going hungry. Multiplying tests the plan, and dividing finds the best one.

maths.problem: Scientists found that a thale cress leaf uses about 95 parts in every 100 of its starch by dawn. A leaf starts the night with 80 units. About how many units are used, and how many are left?
maths.answer: 76 units are used and 4 are left.
maths.explain: 95 parts in 100 is 95 per cent. 10 per cent of 80 is 8, so 5 per cent is 4. Then 80 − 4 = 76. The 4 units left are a small safety margin, in case dawn is a little late.
maths.context: This is about how a leaf uses starch at night. In Dawn Leaf, Dusk Leaf the dawn leaves were pale but often not completely empty.
maths.why_maths: A percentage lets you apply one finding to a leaf of any size. It also shows how small the leftover is.

maths.problem: In Measure the Sun Catcher, three leaves had areas of 12, 18 and 24 square centimetres. The plant has 45 leaves. The round pot is 20 centimetres wide. About how many times bigger is the leaf area than the top of the pot?
maths.explain: Mean leaf area: 12 + 18 + 24 = 54, and 54 ÷ 3 = 18 square centimetres. All the leaves: 18 × 45 = 810 square centimetres. Pot: 20 × 20 = 400, and three quarters of 400 is 300 square centimetres. Then 810 ÷ 300 = 2.7.
maths.context: This is about Measure the Sun Catcher. You trace leaves on squared paper and compare the plant's total leaf area with the area of the pot.
maths.why_maths: A plant catches light with area, not with height or weight. Working out the area shows how much light catcher a small pot plant holds out.

maths.problem: One square metre of paddy field gives about 300 grams of rice in one crop. A child eats about 150 grams of rice a day. About how many square metres of field does the child's rice for one year need?
maths.answer: About 183 square metres, if the field gives one crop a year.
maths.explain: 300 ÷ 150 = 2, so one square metre feeds the child for 2 days. A year has 365 days, and 365 ÷ 2 = 182.5. That rounds up to 183 square metres, which is about the floor of a large flat and a half. The numbers are rounded averages for India.
maths.context: This is about Plate to Sun, where you followed each food on your plate back to a plant catching sunlight. Here you work out how much field that takes.
maths.why_maths: Leaves catch only a small share of the sunlight. Working out the area shows how much green surface stands behind one person's food.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that not all food starts with sunlight? This card tells the true story, and the idea that turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: Until 1977, scientists believed that the deep sea floor was almost empty. No sunlight reaches it, so no plants or algae can grow there. They thought the few animals living there ate only scraps that sank from the sunlit water far above. In February 1977, geologists went down 2,500 metres in a small submarine called Alvin, near the Galápagos Islands. They were looking for hot springs. They found them. Around the springs they also found crowds of animals: clams as big as dinner plates, crabs, and tubeworms taller than a child. Sinking scraps could never feed so many. In 1981 Colleen Cavanaugh, a student at Harvard University, showed that the tubeworms' bodies are packed with bacteria. The bacteria make food using energy from a chemical in the hot water, not from light. This is called chemosynthesis. Sergei Winogradsky had found it in bacteria in 1887, but nobody had expected it to feed whole communities of animals.
how_we_found_out.who: The geologists who dived in Alvin, led by Jack Corliss. Colleen Cavanaugh, who worked out how the tubeworms are fed. Sergei Winogradsky, who first found chemosynthesis in bacteria.
how_we_found_out.when: 1887 (Winogradsky), February 1977 (the dives near the Galápagos Islands) and 1981 (Cavanaugh's paper)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That every community of animals must be fed by sunlight, so the dark sea floor could hold only a few animals living on scraps. The crowded hot springs, and the bacteria inside the tubeworms, showed that chemicals from rock can feed a community too.
how_we_found_out.art: A small white submarine with its lights on, hovering above a dark sea floor crowded with tall tubeworms and large white clams around a hot spring.

roots.context: We have learned how chlorophyll catches light, and how a leaf keeps that energy as starch and spends it through the night. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In Dawn Leaf, Dusk Leaf, the leaves picked at dusk went dark with iodine, and the leaves picked at dawn stayed pale. The starch made by day was spent in the dark, at a speed that made it last until morning. Sunlight comes only by day, but a living being needs energy every hour. So catching light is only half of what a leaf does. The other half is keeping the light's energy and sharing it out through the night.
deep_truth.habit: We say that a plant 'makes food from light', and we picture this happening at noon. That leaves out the night, which is half of a plant's life. We also tend to think that saving and sharing out are things only animals with brains do. A leaf does both every night.
deep_truth.evidence: In Dawn Leaf, Dusk Leaf, leaves from one plant held much more starch at sunset than at sunrise. Scientists who measured thale cress hour by hour found a steady use of starch that ends almost exactly at dawn. When they made the night come four hours early, the plants slowed down and still lasted until dawn.

three.who_am_i: You have no chlorophyll. Every bit of energy you use today was caught by chlorophyll in a leaf or an alga, and kept as starch, sugar or oil until you ate it.
three.what_is_life: Living beings do not only take energy in. They keep it and spend it later. A seed, a potato, a leaf at dusk and the fat under your own skin all hold energy from sunlight, kept for a time with no light.
three.what_is_this_world: Half of the Earth is always in the dark. The whole living world gets through every night on light that was caught during the day.

roots.thread: Light leaves the Sun as one stream of energy. A chlorophyll molecule catches one tiny packet of it. From there the same energy takes many forms. It is in the sugar and starch of a leaf, in a grain of rice, in the muscles of the child who eats the rice, and in the warmth of her skin. The energy is never made and never lost on the way. Each living being holds it for a while and passes it on.

science.text: Energy is never made or destroyed. A plant does not create energy. They change the energy of light into chemical energy, as Julius Robert Mayer wrote in 1845.
Thale cress plants use their leaf starch at a steady rate that lasts until dawn, and change the rate at once when the night is made longer.
How a plant sets that rate, and whether it should be called measuring or dividing, is still argued over.

other_view.view: They say a plant does not plan the night. The speed of starch use is set by chemical reactions tied to the plant's daily clock, which was shaped over millions of years. In this view, 'saving' and 'sharing out' are words that describe people, and we only borrow them for plants.

practice.title: One grain of rice
practice.say: Take one grain of cooked rice and hold it on your palm. Look at it. Now put it on your tongue and chew very slowly. Count to thirty in your head. Notice whether it starts to taste a little sweet. This starch was made in a paddy leaf, by day. The energy in it left the Sun last year. Now close your eyes and feel your next breath. That energy is becoming yours.
practice.kid: Hold one grain of cooked rice. Look at it. Chew it very slowly. Count to thirty. Does it turn a little sweet? A paddy leaf made this starch from light. Close your eyes. Feel your next breath.

ask: A leaf catches light by day and shares out the energy all night. Is the leaf planning? How could anyone tell?
The energy you are using to read this was once sunlight on a leaf. At what point did it become yours?
You have no chlorophyll, and a white patch on a leaf has none. Who are the green cells that feed you?

playtest: The experiments and activities in this lesson were reasoned through step by step. They have not yet been tried at home. Please treat the amounts and times as a starting point. Dawn Leaf, Dusk Leaf (core) needs a plant with thin leaves that gets direct sun, a sunny day, surgical spirit and povidone-iodine. A grown-up must do every step with hot water and spirit, and spirit must never be near a flame. The dusk leaves usually go much darker than the dawn leaves. Some plants do not empty their leaves in one night, so both pairs can look dark. The step says to add a leaf wrapped in foil for two days in that case. If no leaf goes dark, the plant had too little sun or stores little starch, and another plant is needed. Money plant and other thick leaves work badly. The White Patch needs one leaf with truly white patches. Pale yellow-green patches hold some chlorophyll and come out grey. The Banana Clock needs bananas at three stages, and a cooking banana serves as the raw one. Tested slices must not be eaten. The Red Glow works best with a small ultraviolet torch, which is optional to buy. With a white torch the red glow is faint. Green Under Red needs red amaranth, which most vegetable shops sell. Leaf Prints That Fade needs a window that gets direct sun. Behind glass the fading is slower, so the step allows three more days. Starch Bank was played through on paper with two players. With only three nights each way, the die can hide the gain from the working clock. Back to the Sun uses simplified chains. No part of the core path needs a garden. Facts checked on 18 Nov 2026 against memory of the cited papers, not against the papers themselves. A person should check these points: that albino jackfruit seedlings are imagined for the story (albino seedlings are well documented in maize and rice), the 300 grams of rice from one square metre, and the dates in 'Who worked this out'.
